title: Using the CARS vehicle data
text: Preface

title: Using the CARS vehicle data
text:
What this book is for
The CARS project (Connecting Administrative vehicle data for Research on Sustainable transport) has combined three open government datasets, the MOT test results, the MOT history of every vehicle, and the DVLA’s vehicle records, into one research-ready table. It describes 93.4 million vehicles that were on the roads of the United Kingdom at some point between 2005 and 2025. For each vehicle it gives the make, model, fuel, engine size, emissions standard and other characteristics, and, for every year, how far the vehicle was driven and in which postcode area it was tested.
Data like this has not been available before. The UK publishes counts of licensed vehicles, but not how much vehicles are used, area by area, or how the fleet in a place changes as vehicles arrive, age, move away and are scrapped. The CARS data makes those questions answerable, for example:

How far are cars driven in different parts of the country, and is that changing?
How quickly are electric vehicles spreading, and where do they go once their first owner sells them?
How many older diesel vehicles remain in an area that is considering a Clean Air Zone?
How long do vehicles last, and how does their use change with age?

The source data was collected for administration, not research. Making sense of it needs some knowledge of how vehicles are tested, registered and classified in the UK, and an understanding of what the data can and cannot tell you. This book provides both.

title: Using the CARS vehicle data
text:
Who it is for
The book is written for researchers, analysts and policymakers who are intelligent and numerate but not necessarily experts on vehicles or on administrative data. It supports two ways of working:






TipWorking in a spreadsheet



Most questions can be answered from the aggregate tables: CSV files of counts and mileage by postcode area, year, vehicle type and fuel, which open in Excel or any spreadsheet. 12  The aggregate tables describes them and 16  Worked examples: spreadsheets works through examples.








TipWorking in code



The vehicle table (vehicles_enhanced.parquet) has one row per vehicle and is around 9 GB. It is far too large for a spreadsheet, but on an ordinary laptop it can be queried in seconds with DuckDB from R, Python or the command line. 11  The vehicle table describes it and 17  Worked examples: code works through examples.

title: Using the CARS vehicle data
text:
How the book is organised
Part I, Background, explains the vehicle data system in the UK: what an MOT test is (1  The MOT test), which organisations hold which data (2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK), how vehicles are classified (3  Classifying vehicles), fuels and emissions standards (4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards), number plates (5  Number plates), the life of a vehicle from registration to scrapping (6  The life of a vehicle) and the geography the data uses (7  Geography: postcode areas). Readers who know the field can skip it, but the chapters on the life of a vehicle and on geography explain features of the data that catch out even experienced analysts.
Part II, The CARS data, describes where the data comes from and how it was built (8  Source data and linkage, 9  From linked data to research-ready data), what is published (10  Data products and access), the vehicle table and the aggregate tables in detail (11  The vehicle table, 12  The aggregate tables), and how well the data compares with official statistics (13  How good is the data?).
Part III, Using the data, gathers the concepts and pitfalls you need to know before analysing the data (14  Concepts and pitfalls), shows how to get started (15  Getting started), and works through examples in a spreadsheet and in code.
The appendices hold a glossary, the full data dictionary, a catalogue of the aggregate tables, notes on how this book is maintained, and the technical reports produced by the data pipeline.






ImportantRead this before you start



If you read only one chapter, read 14  Concepts and pitfalls. The most common mistakes with this data are not technical: treating where a vehicle was tested as where it is kept, reading the fall in vehicle numbers in the last few years as a real decline, or comparing averages built on different groups of vehicles.

title: 1  The MOT test
text:
1.1 What the MOT test is
Almost everything in the CARS data starts with the MOT test. Each test records a vehicle’s odometer reading and where it was tested, and it is the sequence of tests over a vehicle’s life that lets us estimate how far it is driven each year and where it is kept. Understanding when vehicles are tested, and when they are not, is the key to understanding the data.
The MOT test is the annual roadworthiness check required for most vehicles in Great Britain once they reach three years old. The name comes from the Ministry of Transport, which introduced the test in 1960. At first it applied only to vehicles ten years old or more; the age was lowered in stages, and the first test has been due at three years since 1967.
The test checks that a vehicle meets minimum legal standards for safety and exhaust emissions at the time of the test: brakes, lights, steering, suspension, tyres, seatbelts, structure, emissions and so on. It does not check the general mechanical condition of the engine, clutch or gearbox. Tests are carried out by around 23,000 privately run garages approved as MOT testing stations, under rules set and enforced by the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA; see Chapter 2).
Driving a vehicle that needs an MOT without a valid certificate is an offence, and a valid MOT is required to tax a vehicle. That link to vehicle tax is what makes the MOT such a complete record of the vehicles in use.

title: 1  The MOT test
text:
1.2 What a test records
Since 2005 every MOT test in Great Britain has been recorded electronically. For research the important items are:







Item
Why it matters




Date of the test
Places the vehicle in time; the gaps between tests define the periods over which mileage is measured


Odometer reading
The distance the vehicle has travelled; the difference between two tests gives the distance driven between them


Test result
Pass or fail. A failed vehicle is usually retested within days, so a vehicle can have several tests in a year


Testing station
Where the vehicle was tested. The anonymised data releases the postcode area of the station (Chapter 7)


Test class
The kind of vehicle being tested (Chapter 3)


Vehicle details
Make, model, fuel, engine size, colour and first-use date, as held on the DVSA’s records









ImportantPitfall: the place is the testing station, not the keeper’s home



The postcode area attached to a vehicle in a year is the area of the garage where it was tested. Most people use a garage near home or work, so this is a good guide to where vehicles are kept, but it is not an address. Vehicles kept near the edge of a postcode area, company fleets serviced centrally, and people who have their car tested near work rather than home all blur the picture. See Chapter 7 and Chapter 14.

title: 1  The MOT test
text:
1.3 When a vehicle is tested

The first test
In Great Britain, cars, vans and motorcycles have their first MOT on the third anniversary of their first registration. Some vehicles are tested from their first birthday instead, notably taxis, private hire vehicles, ambulances and passenger vehicles with more than eight passenger seats (Table 3.1 in Chapter 3). In Northern Ireland the first test is at four years.
This has a large effect on the data. For its first three years a vehicle is on the DVLA register, but it has no MOT test. Once it has its first test, the annualisation fills in those early years from it (Chapter 6), so in hindsight the vehicle appears from its first registration. Vehicles that have not yet had a first test have no location at all, which is why the newest vehicles are missing from the last three years of the data. A vehicle that is tested before it is three is usually a taxi, a private hire car or a vehicle with an unusual history, and is driven much further than most.


Later tests
After the first test, a vehicle is tested every year. A vehicle can be tested up to a month (minus a day) before its current certificate expires and keep the same renewal date, so most vehicles are tested at about the same time each year. In practice the intervals vary: tests are taken early or late, failed tests are repeated, and vehicles are taken off the road for a while and then tested again when they return.






NoteTo be written



A short description, with a figure, of the observed distribution of intervals between consecutive tests (from the analysis of test intervals for the linkage stage). The early draft has a heat map of interval start against interval end for 2017–2023, showing the strong annual diagonal, the 2020 disruption and a tail of long gaps.




Vehicles that do not need an MOT
Some vehicles never appear, or stop appearing, in the MOT data even though they are on the road:

Heavy goods vehicles, large buses and coaches, and trailers take a separate annual test run by DVSA, not an MOT. They are largely absent from the CARS data, which is why it describes cars, vans and motorcycles well and heavier vehicles poorly.
Historic vehicles. Since May 2018, most vehicles made more than 40 years ago, and not substantially changed, are exempt. Older vehicles therefore disappear from the MOT data even if they are still driven.
Some other vehicles are exempt, such as tractors and some electric goods vehicles registered before March 2015.

Vehicles declared off the road (SORN), exported or scrapped also stop being tested; Chapter 6 explains how the data handles them.

title: 1  The MOT test
text:
1.4 Disruptions to testing

COVID-19 in 2020
From 30 March 2020, cars, vans and motorcycles whose MOT was due were given a six-month extension, so many vehicles that would normally have been tested in spring and early summer 2020 were not tested until late 2020 or 2021. Vehicles due from 1 August 2020 needed a test again as normal.
Combined with the fall in travel during the lockdowns, this makes 2020 the most unusual year in the data. The fall in average mileage is real, but how it is spread between 2019, 2020 and 2021 depends on how the distance between two tests is shared across the years they span (Chapter 8).








Figure 1.1: Average annual mileage of all vehicles with a recorded mileage, by year. 2025 is a partial year.







Northern Ireland
Northern Ireland has its own testing system, run by the Driver & Vehicle Agency (DVA) at government test centres rather than private garages. In early 2020, before the pandemic, faults found in the vehicle lifts at the test centres led the DVA to suspend many tests and issue temporary exemption certificates, and the pandemic then disrupted testing further. Northern Ireland vehicles are in the CARS data (coded NI), but their test records are less complete than those for Great Britain and their test class is not supplied (Chapter 13).






NoteTo be written



Dates and scale of the Northern Ireland exemptions, and how Northern Ireland test data reaches the DVSA datasets.

title: 1  The MOT test
section: 1.5 What this means for the data
text:
1.5 What this means for the data

The MOT data is a near-complete record of cars, vans and motorcycles aged three and over that are in use.
It largely misses heavy vehicles, historic vehicles and vehicles kept off the road, and, in the last three years of the data, new vehicles that have not yet had their first test.
Location is that of the testing station.
Mileage is measured between tests, so it is known only for periods that have a test at each end, and has to be shared out across calendar years.

title: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK
text:
2.1 The Department for Transport and its agencies
Information about vehicles in the UK is collected by several government bodies, each for its own administrative purpose. Knowing who collects what, and why, explains much of what is in the CARS data and what is missing from it.
The Department for Transport (DfT) is responsible for transport policy. Two of its executive agencies hold the records that CARS draws on, and DfT itself publishes official statistics built from them.
crumbs: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK

title: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK
text:
Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)
The DVLA, based in Swansea, keeps the register of vehicles (and of drivers) for Great Britain, and since 2014 for Northern Ireland as well. Every vehicle used on public roads must be registered. The register records the vehicle’s identity and specification, its registered keeper, and its tax status. The DVLA:

issues the registration number (Chapter 5) and the V5C registration certificate (“logbook”), reissued whenever the keeper or a key detail changes;
collects vehicle excise duty (vehicle tax), whose rates depend on CO2 emissions, fuel and age, which is why the register records these;
records vehicles declared off the road (SORN), exported, or scrapped (Chapter 6).

The keeper’s name and address are personal data and are not published. The DVLA publishes the vehicle details for any registration number through the Vehicle Enquiry Service (VES), used by the public to check a vehicle’s tax and MOT status. CARS uses the VES programming interface (API) to add DVLA details to each vehicle (Chapter 8).


Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA)
The DVSA sets and enforces vehicle testing standards in Great Britain. It runs the MOT scheme (Chapter 1) and the annual test for heavy vehicles, and holds the record of every MOT test. It publishes MOT data in two ways that CARS uses:

the anonymised MOT test data: every test, with the test date, result, odometer reading, test class and postcode area of the testing station, but without the registration number;
the MOT history API, including a bulk download: every registered vehicle, with its registration number, make, model, fuel and dates, and the history of its MOT tests (but no location).



Driver & Vehicle Agency, Northern Ireland (DVA)
Vehicle testing in Northern Ireland is run separately, by the DVA. Its tests reach the DVSA datasets, but Northern Ireland differs from Great Britain in ways that show in the data: the first test is at four years, tests are carried out at government test centres, and the test class is not supplied (Chapter 1).
crumbs: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK

title: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK
text:
2.2 Official statistics
DfT publishes several statistical series about vehicles and their use. They are the natural benchmarks for the CARS data, and CARS uses some of them directly.



Series
What it covers
How it relates to CARS




Vehicle licensing statistics
Counts of licensed and SORN vehicles from the DVLA register, by body type, make, model, fuel, age and area (the VEH tables)
CARS uses DfT’s make and model names (VEH0220, VEH0124) and compares its vehicle counts with DfT’s (Chapter 13)


Road traffic statistics
Vehicle miles travelled on roads, estimated from traffic counts
Measures traffic on the roads of an area, whoever drives it; CARS measures the distance driven by vehicles tested in an area, wherever it is driven


National Travel Survey (NTS)
A household survey of how people travel in England, including car mileage
Survey-based and England only, but links travel to people and households


Anonymised MOT data
Test-level MOT results, published since 2010
One of the CARS sources (Chapter 8)



Other sources often used alongside vehicle data:

The Census (ONS, NRS and NISRA) records the number of cars or vans available to each household, for small areas.
SMMT (the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders) publishes new vehicle registrations by make, model and fuel.

title: 2  Who holds vehicle data in the UK
section: 2.3 Open data and the Open Government Licence
text:
2.3 Open data and the Open Government Licence
The three sources CARS combines are published under the Open Government Licence (OGL). The OGL allows anyone to copy, adapt, combine and republish the information, including commercially, provided the source is acknowledged. Because each source may be used and republished, so may the combination, and the CARS data products are released on the same basis (Chapter 10).
The difficulty with these sources has never been access. It is that they are very large, structured for administration rather than analysis, and not linked to each other. The bulk MOT history download alone is over 400 GB of compressed JSON files. CARS does the linking and restructuring so that others do not have to.

title: 3  Classifying vehicles
text:
3.1 MOT test classes
“Car” seems a simple idea, but the UK uses at least three different ways of dividing vehicles into types, each made for a different purpose and each drawing the boundaries in slightly different places. The CARS data carries all three, so it is worth knowing how they differ.
The MOT test class sets which version of the test a vehicle takes, which depends on what it is and how heavy it is. Most of the vehicles in the data are class 4.
Two features of the classes often surprise people:
In the CARS data, test_class_ANON is the test class as supplied in the anonymised MOT data, and test_class fills its gaps from similar vehicles (Chapter 9). The supplied class is missing for every vehicle in Northern Ireland and for many vehicles never tested.

Class 4 is not “cars”. It includes vans up to 3,000kg, motor caravans, taxis and minibuses with up to 12 passenger seats. It excludes the heaviest vans (3,000–3,500kg), which are class 7.

title: 3  Classifying vehicles
text:
3.2 Type approval categories
Before a new model can be sold, its design must be approved as meeting the rules for its category: crash protection, braking, lighting, emissions and so on. The categories come from international (UN and EU) regulation, carried into GB type approval after the UK left the EU.



Table 3.3: Type approval categories. The L categories are formally written with an “e” (L1e, L3e and so on), and most are divided into subcategories; the limits shown are those of the current regulation (EU 168/2013, retained in GB law).









Category
Vehicles




M1
Passenger vehicles with up to 8 passenger seats: cars, including SUVs and MPVs


M2
Passenger vehicles with more than 8 passenger seats, up to 5 tonnes: minibuses


M3
Passenger vehicles with more than 8 passenger seats, over 5 tonnes: buses and coaches


N1
Goods vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes: vans and pick-ups


N2
Goods vehicles over 3.5 and up to 12 tonnes


N3
Goods vehicles over 12 tonnes


L1
Two-wheeled mopeds: maximum design speed 45 km/h, and an engine up to 50cc or 4 kW


L2
Three-wheeled mopeds, with the same speed and engine limits as L1


L3
Two-wheeled motorcycles: faster than 45 km/h or an engine over 50cc


L4
Motorcycles with a sidecar


L5
Powered tricycles: three wheels, faster or more powerful than an L2 moped


L6
Light quadricycles: four wheels, up to 425 kg and 45 km/h (for example small “microcars” that can be driven at 16)


L7
Heavy quadricycles: four wheels, up to 450 kg (600 kg for goods) and 15 kW, including on-road quad bikes and small city cars such as the Renault Twizy


O
Trailers


T
Agricultural tractors






The type approval category and the MOT class are separate schemes, but the category largely decides the class:

M1 cars take a class 4 MOT.
M2 minibuses take class 4 with up to 12 passenger seats, or class 5 with more: for minibuses, seat count decides.
M3 buses and coaches mostly take the separate annual test.
N1 vans take class 4 up to 3,000kg design gross weight, or class 7 from 3,000kg to 3,500kg: for vans, weight decides.
N2 and N3 goods vehicles take the heavy goods vehicle annual test, not an MOT.

In the CARS data, typeApproval_DVLA is the category as the DVLA register records it, and type_approval fills gaps from similar vehicles. The DVLA records a type approval category for most vehicles registered in recent decades, but rarely for older ones.

Type approval against test class in the data
Table 3.4 counts the vehicles in the vehicle table for each combination of type approval category and MOT test class. The rules above show up clearly in the recorded values:

85.0% of M1 cars are class 4; almost all the rest have no recorded test class.
N1 vans divide between class 4 (56.5%) and class 7 (25.0%), by weight.
M2 minibuses are mostly class 5 (71.2%), with the smaller ones in class 4.
L3 motorcycles divide between class 1 and class 2 by engine size, and L5 tricycles are mostly class 3.
N2 and N3 lorries, M3 buses and coaches, and T tractors almost never have an MOT test class, because they take the annual test or are exempt.

ImportantPitfall: filled values can make impossible combinations



The harmonised type_approval and test_class are each filled from the most common value among similar vehicles, independently of each other. Filling covers far more vehicles, but it also creates combinations the rules do not allow, such as 2,109 M1 cars in class 1 (the motorcycle class). Use the recorded values when the relationship between the two schemes matters.


The DVLA field also holds 20,872 values that are not type approval categories, such as numbers, older national codes and lower-case variants; they are shown as Other code.

title: 3  Classifying vehicles
text:
3.3 DfT body types
DfT’s vehicle licensing statistics divide vehicles into body types:

Cars
Light goods vehicles (LGVs): goods vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes, the N1 category
Motorcycles, including mopeds and scooters
Buses and coaches
Heavy goods vehicles (HGVs)
Other vehicles: tractors, three-wheelers, special vehicles and so on

Body type is the classification CARS uses for most of its tables, because it matches the official statistics. The vehicle table’s body_type column is derived from the vehicle’s make and model, matched to DfT’s names; where the model does not settle it, from the type approval category; and failing that, from the test class (Chapter 9).

title: 3  Classifying vehicles
text:
3.4 How the schemes compare
The schemes draw their lines in different places, which matters whenever CARS results are compared with other statistics:

A class 4 count includes vans up to 3,000kg and minibuses with up to 12 seats; a DfT cars count includes neither.
A DfT light goods vehicles count includes the 3,000–3,500kg vans that are MOT class 7.
Taxis and private hire vehicles are ordinary M1 cars for type approval and DfT, but take their first MOT at one year rather than three.
DfT’s road traffic statistics use their own definitions again, based on how vehicles are recognised in traffic counts.







TipWhich should I use?



For comparisons with DfT statistics, use body_type. For questions about the MOT test itself, or to reproduce earlier CARS outputs, use test_class. The churn tables (Chapter 12) are built on class 4 vehicles, so they include vans and small minibuses alongside cars.

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
text:
4.1 Fuel types
Much of the interest in vehicle data comes from its environmental questions: how fast the fleet is moving to electric, how many older polluting vehicles remain, and what this means for carbon emissions and air quality. This chapter explains the fuel and emissions information in the data and its limits.
“Electric vehicle” is used loosely. Policy often groups battery electric, plug-in hybrid and range-extended vehicles as plug-in vehicles, or uses ultra low emission vehicle (ULEV) for vehicles emitting under 75g of CO2 per km. Always check which definition a statistic uses.
crumbs: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
text:
Fuel
What it means




Petrol and diesel
Conventional internal combustion engines


Hybrid electric
A petrol or diesel engine with an electric motor and battery. Mild hybrids use a small motor to assist the engine; full hybrids (such as the Toyota Prius) can drive short distances on electricity alone. Neither can be plugged in: the battery is charged by the engine and by braking


Plug-in hybrid electric (PHEV)
A hybrid with a larger battery that can be charged from the mains, giving a useful electric-only range, typically 20–50 miles


Range-extended electric
An electric vehicle with a small engine that only charges the battery


Battery electric (BEV)
Electric only, charged from the mains, with no engine


Fuel cell
Electric drive powered by a hydrogen fuel cell; very rare


Gas
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), compressed or liquefied natural gas (CNG, LNG); usually conversions of petrol or diesel vehicles





How fuel is recorded
The DVSA and the DVLA each record a fuel, using different labels, and neither distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from any other hybrid: DVSA records Hybrid Electric (Clean) for mild, full and plug-in petrol hybrids alike. DfT’s vehicle licensing statistics do distinguish them, by model.
CARS keeps both supplied fuels (fuel_DVSA, fuelType_DVLA) and builds a harmonised fuel from them: the DVSA fuel, corrected where the DVLA record or the engine size shows it is wrong (for example a Toyota Prius recorded as Electric), and with plug-in hybrids identified from DfT’s records for the vehicle’s model (Chapter 9). fuel_simple groups it into six:

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
text:
4.2 Engine size
Engine size is the capacity of the engine’s cylinders in cubic centimetres (cc). It is a rough guide to a vehicle’s power and fuel use. A battery electric vehicle has no engine: in the harmonised engine_cc its engine size is 0, and tables that band engine size give it its own band.
crumbs: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
text:
4.3 CO2 emissions
The CO2 figure (co2, in grams per kilometre) is the official value measured when the model was type approved, not a measurement of the individual vehicle. It is recorded because vehicle tax for cars registered since March 2001 depends on it, so it is mostly missing for older vehicles.






ImportantPitfall: two test procedures



CO2 figures were measured on the NEDC laboratory test until it was replaced by the more realistic WLTP test, from September 2017 for new models and September 2018 for all new cars. WLTP figures are typically higher for the same vehicle, so a rise in recorded CO2 around 2018 is partly an artefact of the change of test. Official figures also understate real-world emissions, by different amounts in different periods.


A recorded CO2 of zero is only kept for vehicles with no engine; elsewhere it is treated as missing (Chapter 9).
crumbs: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
text:
4.4 Euro emission standards
Euro standards limit the air pollutants a new vehicle may emit: nitrogen oxides (NOx), particulate matter, carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons. (They do not limit CO2.) Each new standard is stricter than the last, and applies to new type approvals first and, a year or so later, to every new vehicle registered.

Standards for cars, vans and motorcycles are written in Arabic numerals: Euro 1 to Euro 6. Euro 6 has sub-stages (6b, 6c, 6d-TEMP, 6d, 6e) that tightened testing, including real driving emissions (RDE) tests on the road.
Standards for lorries and buses are written in Roman numerals: Euro I to Euro VI. They are separate regulations measured on a different basis.

The CARS column euro_standard puts both on one numeric scale (1 to 6), which is convenient, but a Euro 6 car and a Euro VI bus meet different limits.

title: 4  Fuels, emissions and Euro standards
section: 4.5 Clean Air Zones and low emission zones
text:
4.5 Clean Air Zones and low emission zones
Several UK cities charge or restrict the most polluting vehicles in Clean Air Zones (CAZ), and London has its Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ). The usual minimum standards are Euro 4 for petrol cars and vans, Euro 6 for diesel cars and vans, and Euro VI for buses, coaches and lorries.
Because recorded Euro status was so sparse, the CARS churn tables (Set 7, Chapter 12) use the vehicle’s first-use date as a proxy: petrol vehicles first used before 2006, and diesel vehicles first used before 2015, are counted as likely non-compliant.

title: 5  Number plates
text:
5.1 Formats
Every vehicle registered in the UK has a vehicle registration mark (VRM), usually called its registration number or number plate (in other countries a licence plate). The VRM is how the CARS sources are joined, and its format says when and, for recent vehicles, where the vehicle was first registered.
The rules for displaying plates are on GOV.UK.
Great Britain has used four main formats. Northern Ireland has its own.
There are also Q plates, for vehicles whose age or identity cannot be established (for example kit cars or rebuilt vehicles), and formats for diplomatic vehicles, the Isle of Man, the Channel Islands and foreign registrations.

title: 5  Number plates
text:
5.2 Personalised plates
Registration numbers can be bought and transferred between vehicles, and cherished or personalised plates are popular. A vehicle can carry a plate that makes it look older than it is, but never younger: a 2015 car can carry a 1990 H plate, but not a 2020 20 plate. Dateless and Northern Ireland plates are popular for this, because they hide the vehicle’s age altogether.
Transfers affect the data in two ways:

The plate’s date and the vehicle’s age disagree. CARS decodes each plate and flags vanity_plate when the vehicle’s birth date falls outside the plate’s issue period. The flag catches any mismatch, not only personalised plates: imported vehicles, Q plates and re-registered vehicles are flagged too.
A registration number can belong to different vehicles at different times. When a plate moves, a lookup by registration number returns the vehicle that carries it now. This is the main reason a DVLA record can describe a different vehicle from the DVSA record it was matched to (Chapter 9).

title: 6  The life of a vehicle
text:
6.1 Stages of a vehicle’s life
The CARS data follows each vehicle through its life, year by year. To read it correctly you need to know the stages a vehicle passes through, which ones leave a trace in the data, and how the data describes the years in which a vehicle is not seen.
crumbs: 6  The life of a vehicle

title: 6  The life of a vehicle
text:
A new vehicle
A new vehicle is registered with the DVLA when it is first sold, or sometimes earlier by a dealer (pre-registration), and receives its registration number. Its date of first registration is recorded by the DVLA and its first-use date by DVSA; the two are usually the same. The manufacture date can be months earlier for a vehicle that sat in stock.
For its first three years (four in Northern Ireland) a new vehicle needs no MOT. Until its first test, the MOT data knows it exists but not where it is or how far it has been driven. Once it has been tested, the annualisation fills in its early years from that first test (see below).


An imported vehicle
A used vehicle imported into the UK is registered when it arrives. It is given a plate for its age, where its age can be shown, or a Q plate where it cannot (Chapter 5). Its UK registration date can therefore be many years after it was built, which affects anything inferred from dates, such as its Euro standard (Chapter 4).


The first MOT
At three years old the vehicle has its first MOT (Chapter 1), and from then on it is observed at least once a year: its location (the postcode area of the test station) and its odometer reading. The first test also gives the first measurement of how far it has been driven: the whole distance since new.






NoteTo be written



Whether the data can identify vehicles tested before their third birthday (taxis, private hire vehicles and others), and how they appear in the mileage figures.




Off the road: SORN
A keeper who takes a vehicle off the road, and stops taxing and insuring it, must make a Statutory Off Road Notification (SORN). A SORN vehicle may not be driven or parked on a public road, and needs no MOT. A SORN lasts until the vehicle is taxed again, sold or scrapped.
A SORN vehicle therefore drops out of the MOT data, and reappears if it returns to the road. Many old vehicles stay on SORN for years, which is why DfT’s counts, which include SORN vehicles, hold more old vehicles than the MOT data (Chapter 13).






NoteTo be written



The history of SORN rules: when SORN was introduced, and the period when a SORN had to be renewed every twelve months rather than lasting indefinitely (possible sources: DVLA SORN myths, Impact assessment 2013/188).




Export
A vehicle sold abroad is marked for export and leaves the UK register. The DVLA records the marker (markedForExport_DVLA, ever_export_marked).


End of life
A vehicle at the end of its life is taken to an authorised treatment facility, which issues a certificate of destruction and tells the DVLA. A vehicle that is badly damaged may be written off by its insurer, and either scrapped or repaired and returned to the road. Some vehicles are stolen and never recovered.
crumbs: 6  The life of a vehicle

title: 6  The life of a vehicle
section: 6.2 How the data describes a vehicle’s life
text:
6.2 How the data describes a vehicle’s life
For every year from 2005 to 2025 the vehicle table has a column pca_YYYY. Where the annualisation could place the vehicle, it holds a postcode area. Otherwise it holds one of three statuses:







Status
Meaning




a postcode area (e.g. LS)
Observed: the vehicle is placed in this area that year


unborn
The vehicle had not yet been first registered (its birth year is this year or later)


unknown
The vehicle existed, but was not placed: for example a new vehicle that has not yet had its first MOT, or a long gap between tests


dead
The year is after the vehicle’s last MOT and beyond the years its postcode area is carried forward









ImportantPitfall: observed does not mean tested that year



The annualisation gives a vehicle a postcode area in years when it was not tested:

before its first MOT, the postcode area of the first test is copied back to the years since its first registration;
after its last MOT, the postcode area is carried forward for about two years.

So a vehicle is observed from its first registration, once it has been tested, until about two years after its last test. A vehicle scrapped soon after its last MOT therefore stays observed for about two more years. The pipeline’s quality/pca_observation_by_year.csv counts, for each year, the observed vehicles that were past their last MOT or under three.








NoteTo be confirmed



The exact rules for copying the postcode area back from the first test and forward from the last, from the linkage stage.










Figure 6.1: Vehicles in the CARS vehicle table by their status in each year.





Every vehicle is in exactly one status each year, so the four lines in Figure 6.1 always add up to the same total: every vehicle in the table. The observed line peaks before the end of the series and then falls. That fall is not a shrinking fleet. Vehicles first registered in the last three years mostly have not had a first MOT yet, so they are unknown, and the last year, 2025, is incomplete.






ImportantPitfall: dead means no longer tested, not scrapped



A vehicle is dead in every year after its last MOT, whatever the reason: scrapped, exported, declared SORN, exempt as a historic vehicle, or simply driven illegally without a test. The data cannot tell these apart. A vehicle that comes back from SORN after a gap is unknown in the gap, not dead, because the status is set from the date of its last test.








ImportantPitfall: the recent years look like vehicles are vanishing



A vehicle tested for the last time in 2023 might be dead, or might simply be late for its test. Near the end of the series the data cannot yet tell, so a vehicle last seen in either of the final two years is usually left unknown rather than dead. Treat counts of vehicles leaving the fleet in the last two or three years with care.
crumbs: 6  The life of a vehicle

title: 6  The life of a vehicle
text:
6.3 Within-year flags from the annualisation
The annualisation (Chapter 8) also sets, for each year, flags describing where the vehicle was in its life on 1 July, the straddle date used to assign each year:

is_new_vehicle: in its first-use period, before its first MOT;
is_intertest: between two MOT tests, with a test either side of 1 July that are no more than two years apart;
is_end_use: in its last period, after its final MOT.

The flags are blank before the vehicle is born, more than a year after its last test, and when the tests either side of 1 July are more than two years apart. Take a vehicle first used in September 2007 whose first test on record is in 2013, with later tests in 2014, 2016, 2018 and every year from 2020. It went six years without a test, and there are gaps of 26 months (2016 to 2018: too long, so is_intertest is blank) and 23 months (2018 to 2020: under two years, so is_intertest is TRUE).
Mileage is still shared out across every year between two tests, however long the gap. The flags describe the evidence, not whether a mileage exists.
The CARS pipeline uses these flags to find each vehicle’s last MOT year (and so when it becomes dead), and then drops them from the published vehicle table.






NoteTo be written



Confirm the exact definitions of the three flags, and whether they should be published.
crumbs: 6  The life of a vehicle

title: 7  Geography: postcode areas
text:
7.1 Postcodes and postcode areas
The only location in the CARS data is the postcode area (PCA) of the testing station where the vehicle had its MOT. This chapter explains what postcode areas are, how they relate to other geographies, and the limits of analysing vehicles at this scale.
Postcodes were first used in London in the 1850s and 1860s, with districts named by compass point (N, E, SW and so on), and later extended to some large provincial cities. The current national system was rolled out between the 1950s and the 1970s. Postcodes are designed by Royal Mail for one purpose: to sort and deliver mail efficiently.
A full postcode such as LS2 9JT has four nested levels:
The area is the one or two letters at the start, usually from the name of the main town or city: LS for Leeds, B for Birmingham, G for Glasgow, L for Liverpool. The CARS data has 119 postcode areas. In the data, Northern Ireland is coded NI rather than its real postcode area BT, and a small number of vehicles have the code XX, which is not a real area.
Figure 7.1: Average annual mileage of cars by postcode area, 2022 (plausible mileage only). Northern Ireland is shown as a single area.

title: 7  Geography: postcode areas
section: 7.2 How postcode areas differ from other geographies
text:
7.2 How postcode areas differ from other geographies
Postcode areas are large and very uneven. In 2022 the largest held 1,178,874 observed cars (Birmingham) and the smallest 13,012 (Lerwick). They mix cities with their rural hinterlands, and they do not line up with the geographies most other statistics use:

Census geographies (output areas, nested in LSOAs, nested in MSOAs in England and Wales, with equivalents elsewhere) are designed to hold populations of similar size and character.
Administrative geographies (wards, local authority districts, counties and regions) are the units of local government and policy.
Travel to work areas (228 in the UK) are built from commuting flows.

Because postcode boundaries do not follow any of these, linking postcode area data to a local authority or a census area is always a best fit. The usual method is to assign each unit postcode to the area containing its centroid, using the ONS Postcode Directory, and then to aggregate. Some addresses, and so some vehicles, inevitably fall in the “wrong” area.






NoteTo be written



A map of local authority districts overlaid on postcode areas (the early draft had one), and a recommended lookup from postcode areas to local authorities and regions, with its coverage.

title: 7  Geography: postcode areas
section: 7.3 The limits of analysis by postcode area
text:
7.3 The limits of analysis by postcode area

Where vehicles are tested is not where they are kept
The postcode area is that of the testing station, not the keeper’s address. For most private vehicles the two are close, but:

vehicles kept near a postcode area boundary may be tested on either side of it;
people may have their vehicle tested near work rather than home;
fleet and company vehicles may be tested wherever the fleet is maintained;
a vehicle tested in a different area from last year has not necessarily moved: it may simply have gone to a different garage.

The CARS churn tables count a change of area between years as a move, and should be read with this in mind.


The modifiable areal unit problem
Any analysis of data aggregated to areas is affected by the modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP). It has two parts:

The scale effect. Results change with the size of the areas. Average car mileage or vehicle ownership calculated for small areas such as LSOAs varies far more than the same measure calculated for postcode areas, because the large areas average together places that are very different. Low-mileage city centres disappear when they are combined with their higher-mileage hinterlands.
The zoning effect. Different ways of drawing areas of the same size from the same small units can give different results, because any particular set of boundaries is arbitrary. Postcode areas, drawn for mail delivery, have no reason to separate places with different travel behaviour.

Aggregation also brings the ecological fallacy: a relationship seen between areas need not hold for the people or vehicles within them, and can even be reversed. It is easy to find correlations between area averages that are negligible at the level of individual vehicles.






ImportantPitfall: within-area variation can exceed between-area variation



Postcode areas give reliable counts, because they are large. But the differences between areas can be smaller than the differences within them, so an area average may describe very few of the vehicles in it. Use postcode area results to compare places at a broad scale, not to describe neighbourhoods.








NoteTo be written



A worked illustration of the smoothing effect, comparing mileage mapped by LSOA (from MOT-based small-area estimates) and by postcode area with the same colour breaks, and a measure of how much variance is lost by aggregation.




Do patterns between areas mean anything?
One check on whether area-level differences are signal rather than noise is spatial autocorrelation: whether neighbouring areas have more similar values than distant ones. An early analysis of car mileage by postcode area found some, but limited, clustering. The clearest cluster is London, where mileage is low, which confirms that the data behaves as expected but is not in itself a new finding.






NoteTo be written



The spatial autocorrelation analysis (global and local Moran’s I) with its figures, and references.

title: 8  Source data and linkage
text:
8.1 The three sources
The CARS data is built in two stages. The first links the three source datasets and turns each vehicle’s test history into annual figures. The pipeline then cleans and enhances the result and produces the published tables (Chapter 9). This chapter describes the sources and the linkage stage.
All three are published under the Open Government Licence (Chapter 2).

title: 8  Source data and linkage
text:
Anonymised MOT test data
Every MOT test since 2005: the date, result, odometer reading, test class and the postcode area of the testing station, with the vehicle’s make, model, fuel, engine size and first-use date. Vehicles carry an anonymous identifier rather than their registration number. The data was first published by DfT in 2010 and is now published by DVSA, roughly annually; in recent years over 40 million tests a year are added.
Gives CARS: the location of each test, and the test class.


DVSA MOT history (bulk download)
Every vehicle registered in Great Britain, including those not yet tested, with its registration number, make, model, fuel, engine size, colour, dates of first use, registration and manufacture, and its full MOT history: every test with its date, result and odometer reading. There is no location. The download is available through the MOT history API to anyone who applies for a key, and is a set of zipped JSON files of over 400 GB.
Gives CARS: the registration number, which links to the DVLA, and the backbone of one record per vehicle.


DVLA Vehicle Enquiry Service
The DVLA’s Vehicle Enquiry Service API returns, for one registration number at a time, the vehicle’s details from the DVLA register: make, colour, fuel, engine capacity, CO2 emissions, Euro status, type approval category, revenue weight, wheel plan, tax status and due date, MOT status and expiry, year of manufacture, month of first registration, whether it is marked for export, and the date of the latest V5C.
Gives CARS: the emissions and specification details that DVSA does not hold, and evidence of whether and when the vehicle was taxed, declared SORN or exported.

title: 8  Source data and linkage
section: 8.2 Linking the anonymised MOT data to the MOT history
text:
8.2 Linking the anonymised MOT data to the MOT history
The anonymised test data has the location but no registration number; the MOT history has the registration number but no location. The two are linked through the tests themselves: the sequence of test dates and odometer readings of a vehicle is, in practice, a unique fingerprint. Matching fingerprints attaches the postcode area of each test to the vehicle in the MOT history.






NoteTo be written



The fingerprint matching method: which fields are used, how ties and partial matches are resolved, and the match rate.

title: 8  Source data and linkage
text:
8.3 Linking the DVLA records
DVLA details were collected by querying the Vehicle Enquiry Service for every registration number in the DVSA download, many of them several times between 2024 and 2026. Each query returns the vehicle that carries that registration at the time of the query. Because registrations can move between vehicles (Chapter 5), a query does not always describe the same vehicle as the DVSA record with that registration, so we built rules to decide which DVSA vehicle each returned record belongs to.















Figure 8.1: Draft flowchart of the rules for attaching Vehicle Enquiry Service records to DVSA vehicles, with approximate counts at each step (June 2026).



The pipeline adds a further check, comparing the make, year and engine size of the DVSA and DVLA records, and does not use DVLA values where they clearly describe a different vehicle (Chapter 9).






NoteTo be written



A description of the VES linking rules to accompany the flowchart, and of the VES status categories: data returned; invalid registration that will never return data; invalid registration with a proposed cleaned version that does; vehicle not found, assumed to have left the register long ago; vehicle not found now but found at some point; never queried.

title: 8  Source data and linkage
text:
8.4 Annualisation
The tests of a vehicle happen on whatever dates they happen. For analysis it is far more useful to have one figure per vehicle per calendar year. The annualisation converts each vehicle’s test history into, for each year from 2005 to 2025:

mileage_YYYY: the distance driven in the year, in miles;
legit_mileage_YYYY: whether that mileage is plausible;
pca_YYYY: the postcode area the vehicle is assigned to in the year;
flags describing the vehicle’s stage of life in the year (Chapter 6).


Annual mileage
The odometer readings at two consecutive tests give the distance driven between them. That distance is shared across the calendar years the interval spans, however long the interval, so a year can only have a mileage if it is covered by an interval with an odometer reading at each end.






NoteTo be confirmed



How the distance is shared between years (we understand it to be in proportion to the time in each, so an interval from March 2018 to March 2019 contributes most of its distance to 2018), and how the distance before the first test is treated.










Figure 8.2: Draft figure: the date of the test at the start of each interval between tests, against the test at its end, for a sample of vehicles, 2017–2023. Most intervals lie on the one-year diagonal. The disruption in 2020 shows as a break and a shifted line.







Plausible mileage
Odometer readings contain errors: typing mistakes, odometers replaced or reset, readings in kilometres taken as miles, and occasional fraud (clocking). The annualisation judges whether each annual mileage is plausible, and removes the mileage where it is not. legit_mileage_YYYY therefore has three states: TRUE (plausible), blank with a mileage (not assessed) and FALSE (judged implausible; the mileage is then blank).






NoteTo be written



The rules for judging mileage plausible, including the thresholds on miles per day, the treatment of odometer units and resets, and what share of readings each rule removes.




Postcode area in each year
A vehicle is assigned the postcode area of the test closest in time to the year for which a postcode area is available. Years with no test nearby have no postcode area, and the pipeline then labels them unborn, unknown or dead (Chapter 6).






NoteTo be written



The exact rule for choosing the test that gives a year its postcode area, and how many years it can reach across.

title: 8  Source data and linkage
text:
8.5 What the linkage stage produces
The output of the linkage stage is one table with one row per vehicle, 138,238,617 rows in the delivery the current data is built from, and around 200 columns: the DVSA vehicle details, the per-year columns, the attached DVLA columns, and columns recording the history of the DVLA lookups. It is the input to the pipeline described in Chapter 9. It is not itself published (Chapter 10).

title: 9  From linked data to research-ready data
text:
9.1 Principles
The linked table from the linkage stage (Chapter 8) is accurate to its sources, but not yet easy to analyse. The same make is spelt dozens of ways, attributes are missing for many vehicles, and some DVLA records belong to another vehicle. The pipeline, MOT-pipline, cleans and enhances the table and produces the published outputs. This chapter summarises what it does; the full method, with every rule and count, is in the pipeline’s Methodology, included as an appendix.
Four principles run through the pipeline, and they shape how the data should be used:
crumbs: 9  From linked data to research-ready data

title: 9  From linked data to research-ready data
text:
Supplied values are never overwritten. Cleaned, harmonised or filled values go in new columns next to the originals. fuel_DVSA is the fuel as DVSA supplied it; fuel is the harmonised fuel.
Every inferred value records its source. Columns ending _src, _method and _check say how each value was reached, so you can always separate what was recorded from what was inferred.
Weak evidence is flagged, not acted on. A value is changed only when the vehicle’s own records disagree and a second source settles it.
Results are reproducible. Every step is a rule (no language model or random element is used), and rebuilding from the same input gives the same output.
crumbs: 9  From linked data to research-ready data

title: 9  From linked data to research-ready data
text:
9.2 The stages





flowchart TD
    A[Linked and annualised<br/>vehicle table] --> B[1. Core table<br/>scope, dates, yearly status]
    B --> C[2. Make and model<br/>matched to DfT names]
    T[DfT vehicle licensing<br/>statistics] --> C
    A --> M[3a. DVSA-DVLA<br/>record check]
    C --> F[3b. Fuel and engine checks]
    M --> F
    F --> D[3c. Fill gaps from<br/>similar vehicles]
    D --> E[4. Vehicle table<br/>vehicles_enhanced.parquet]
    E --> G[Churn tables]
    E --> H[Mileage and fleet<br/>profile tables]
    E --> I[Quality reports]







1. Core table: which vehicles, and their dates
The input holds 138,238,617 vehicles, many of which left the roads long before 2005. The pipeline keeps every vehicle with evidence that it existed from 2005 onwards: a recorded mileage or postcode area in any year, a birth date from 2005, or DVLA activity (tax, V5C, MOT expiry or first registration) since 2005. That leaves 93,352,241 vehicles. The scope_* columns record which evidence each vehicle has.
It also sets each vehicle’s birth_date (the earliest of its first-use, registration and manufacture dates) and first_use_date, and fills the blank years of pca_YYYY with the statuses unborn, unknown and dead (Chapter 6).


2. Make and model
DVSA records make and model as free text, entered at the test station. “FORD FIESTA ZETEC CLIMATE”, “Fiesta” and “MOMDEO” all occur. The pipeline matches each distinct make and model to the names DfT uses in its vehicle licensing statistics, through a sequence of rules (exact match, generic name, prefix, words, spelling fixes) that each record how they matched:







Column
Example




make_final
FORD


model_final
FIESTA (DfT’s generic model)


derivative_final
ZETEC CLIMATE: the rest of the model text


dft_genmodel
FORD FIESTA, for joining to DfT tables


make_method, model_method, model_confidence
How the match was made, and how sure it is



Using DfT’s names means CARS results can be joined to and compared with the official statistics. The DfT scheme is sometimes coarser than a buyer would use (DfT’s DISCOVERY includes the Discovery Sport), and the derivative keeps the detail. The match also gives each vehicle a DfT body_type (Chapter 3).


3. Checking and harmonising attributes
Eight attributes are harmonised: given one best value per vehicle from the DVSA record, the DVLA record and, where both are missing, similar vehicles. They are fuel, engine_cc, co2, euro_status, type_approval, revenue_weight, wheelplan and test_class.

Is the DVLA record the same vehicle? The make, year and engine size of the DVSA and DVLA records are compared. Where two or more disagree (dvla_match = 'different'), the DVLA record is taken to describe another vehicle and none of its values is used.
Fuel is taken from the records and never filled from other vehicles. DVLA’s fuel is used where DVSA says “Other”, or where DVSA says Electric for a vehicle that has an engine. Plug-in hybrids are identified from DfT’s records for the model (Chapter 4). fuel_check compares each vehicle’s fuel with others of its make and model, and flags rare fuels.
Engine size is 0 for electric vehicles.
Gaps in the other attributes are filled with the most common value among vehicles of the same make, model, birth year and fuel (and engine size where known). Values are never borrowed across fuels.
Euro status that is still missing is assumed from the standard compulsory when the vehicle was made (Chapter 4).

To check that a result does not depend on filled values, repeat it using only recorded ones: filter on co2_src = 'dvla', euro_status_src = 'dvla', engine_cc_src IN ('dvsa', 'dvla') and so on, or use the supplied columns (co2Emissions_DVLA, euroStatus_DVLA). Chapter 17 has an example.

The registration number is decoded to its format, issue period and issuing office, and flagged where it does not match the vehicle’s age (Chapter 5). Simplified groupings such as fuel_simple and euro_standard are added.

9.3 Validation
The pipeline has unit tests for every rule, a set of cross-checks run on every build that compare published numbers that must agree, comparisons with DfT’s statistics (Chapter 13), and a record of an end-to-end audit. See the MOT-pipline repository for details.

title: 10  Data products and access
text:
10.1 Aggregate tables
CARS releases its data as a family of products at different levels of detail. Choose the least detailed product that answers your question: the aggregate tables are much easier to work with, and have already dealt with several of the pitfalls described in Chapter 14.
The aggregate tables count vehicles and sum their mileage by postcode area and year, broken down by body type, fuel, age, engine size and other characteristics. There are three families, described in Chapter 12 and catalogued in Appendix B:
Vehicles that cannot be located in a year are included in the tables under the statuses unknown, dead and unborn, so totals can be reconciled.

title: 10  Data products and access
10  Data products and access
text:
10.2 The vehicle table
vehicles_enhanced.parquet has one row for each of the 93.4 million vehicles in scope, and 272 columns, including 21 years each of mileage, plausibility flag and postcode area. It is described in Chapter 11, and every column is listed in the data dictionary.

title: 10  Data products and access
text:
10.3 The linked source table
The linked and annualised table (Chapter 8), from which the vehicle table is built, holds every vehicle in the DVSA download, including those that left the roads before 2005.






NoteTo be written



Whether, how and to whom the linked source table, the test-level linked data, and an anonymised vehicle-level product without registration numbers will be released.

title: 10  Data products and access
text:
10.4 Licensing and conditions of use
The sources are published under the Open Government Licence v3.0, which permits combining and republishing them, and the CARS products are released on the same basis.






NoteTo be written



The licence of each product, the attribution statement users must include (“Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0”), and any conditions of use.



Registration numbers and personal data
The vehicle table includes each vehicle’s registration number, because it is the key for linking to other data. A registration number is not in itself personal information, and all the sources are published openly. However, a registration number can in some circumstances be linked to a person, and so can be personal data under data protection law.
The project’s approach is that if a way to re-identify individuals from the data is found, the project will:

tell the data owners;
store the data at a level of security suitable for the sensitivity discovered;
make the data and code available only at a suitable level of safeguarding, following the tiered access used by the UK Data Service.

Users must not attempt to identify individuals or their vehicles’ keepers from the data.

title: 10  Data products and access
text:
10.5 Where to get the data






NoteTo be written



The download location of each product (currently the MOT-pipline repository, which will be made public), the archive where versioned releases will be deposited, and their DOIs.

title: 10  Data products and access
text:
10.6 Versions
The data will be revised as the method improves and new MOT data is added. Each build of the pipeline records its versions in session_info.csv, and this book states the build it describes in its preface.






ImportantPitfall: vehicle_id changes between versions



vehicle_id is the row number in the input file and changes whenever a new delivery is processed. To match vehicles across versions, or to other data, use registration_DVSA.

title: 11  The vehicle table
text:
11.1 Parquet
The vehicle table, vehicles_enhanced.parquet, is the most detailed CARS product: one row for each of 93,352,241 vehicles, with 272 columns. This chapter explains how it is organised and how to read it. Every column is described in the data dictionary.
The table is stored as a Parquet file, a compressed column-based format designed for large tables. You do not need to load the whole file to use it: tools such as DuckDB read only the columns and rows a query needs, so a count of vehicles by fuel reads a few hundred megabytes, not 9 GB, and takes seconds. Chapter 15 explains how to set this up.

title: 11  The vehicle table
section: 11.2 One row per vehicle, one column per year
text:
11.2 One row per vehicle, one column per year

title: 11  The vehicle table
text:
11.5 Completeness
The table keeps vehicles for which little is known, rather than dropping them, so how complete a column is varies a great deal. The data dictionary gives the share missing for every column. Some patterns to know:

DVSA columns are nearly complete, because every vehicle comes from the DVSA download. engineSize_DVSA is the exception, missing for 17.11%.
DVLA columns are missing for about 23% of vehicles, those for which no DVLA record was found. Most of these left the register years ago. Some DVLA fields are rare even when a record exists: euroStatus_DVLA is missing for 85.43%.
The harmonised columns fill most gaps: co2 is missing for 25.99% against 38% for co2Emissions_DVLA, and euro_status for 0% against 85.43%.
Year-by-year columns are blank in most years for most vehicles, because a vehicle is only on the road for part of the period. mileage_2019 is blank for 58.59% of vehicles.

title: 11  The vehicle table
text:
11.6 The vehicles included
A vehicle is included if there is evidence that it existed at any point from 2005 (Chapter 9). The table therefore includes vehicles that were scrapped in 2006, vehicles first registered in 2025 that have never been tested, and everything in between. Any analysis of a particular year must first select the vehicles relevant to that year, usually those observed in it: those with a real postcode area in pca_YYYY.

title: 12  The aggregate tables
text:
12.1 Ideas common to all the tables
The aggregate tables are CSV files that open in any spreadsheet. They answer most common questions without the vehicle table, and they have been built so that results can be combined correctly. This chapter explains the three families of table and the ideas common to all of them. Appendix B lists every file, and each family has a detailed report among the appendices.

title: 12  The aggregate tables
text:
Grain
Each table has a grain: the combination of columns that identifies one row. mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv has one row per year, postcode area, body type and fuel group. Knowing the grain tells you what you can add up: you can sum its rows over fuel groups to get totals by body type, or over postcode areas to get national totals.


Long and wide
Most tables come in long form, with one row per combination and one column per measure, which is best for filtering and pivot tables. Some are also given in wide form, with years (or categories) as columns, which is easier to read and chart. They hold the same numbers.


Counts and totals, not just averages
Where a table gives an average, it also gives the count and total it was calculated from (for example n_legit_mileage and total_legit_mileage).






ImportantPitfall: never average the averages



To get the average mileage of a group of rows, add up their totals and divide by the sum of their counts. Taking the average of the rows’ averages gives each row equal weight, so a postcode area with 2,000 cars counts as much as one with 2 million. Chapter 16 shows the right way in Excel.




Status rows
Postcode area columns include the statuses unborn, unknown and dead as well as real areas, so a table’s rows add up to every vehicle in the vehicle table. For most analyses, filter out the status rows to keep the vehicles observed in each year. Be aware that the share of vehicles that are unknown grows towards the end of the series (Chapter 6).


Plausible mileage
Mileage is reported both in full and for plausible mileage only (Chapter 8). Averages should normally use plausible mileage, as the CARS reports do.

title: 12  The aggregate tables
text:
12.2 Mileage tables
Folder tables/mileage/ · report: Vehicles and mileage by postcode area
Vehicles and their annual mileage, for every MOT test class and body type. The most useful single table is mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv, with 52,861 rows: for each year, postcode area (or status), DfT body type and fuel group, it gives:







Column
Meaning




n_vehicles
Vehicles

Vehicles with a recorded, and with a plausible, mileage


n_mileage_removed
Vehicles whose mileage was judged implausible and removed

Total miles, all recorded and plausible only

Vehicles with unusual mileages


n_with_age, total_age
For calculating average age



The other mileage tables give the same information by age, by MOT test class and by the fuel as DVSA supplied it, and the distribution of mileage in bands.

title: 12  The aggregate tables
text:
12.3 Fleet profile tables
Folder tables/profile/ · report: Fleet profile tables
The make-up of the fleet in each year, for cars, light goods vehicles, motorcycles and buses, by characteristics such as fuel, engine size, CO2 band, Euro standard, age band and (for cars) SMMT body type, with the vehicle count and mean mileage of each. They come in long form (profile_categorical_by_year.csv) and in four wide analyses per body type:

Analysis 1 (a1_counts_*): vehicles, years by characteristic;
Analysis 2 (a2_mean_mileage_*): mean mileage, years by characteristic;
Analyses 3 and 4: the same, split by age band.

These tables cover Great Britain only (Northern Ireland is excluded) and count a vehicle in a year only if it has a plausible mileage that year.

title: 12  The aggregate tables
text:
12.4 Churn tables
Folder tables/churn/ · report: Churn tables
The churn tables describe how the vehicles in each postcode area change: which vehicles stay, which arrive from elsewhere or new, and which leave by moving or by ceasing to be tested. They cover MOT test class 4 vehicles: cars, vans up to 3,000kg and small minibuses. They are organised in numbered sets:



Table 12.1: The churn table sets









Set
Question




0
Where did each vehicle’s first-use date come from?


1

2

3
What is each area’s 2017 stock made of: stayers, arrivals and leavers either side?


4

5
Does moving area go with a change in mileage?


6

7

ImportantPitfall: a ‘move’ is a change of testing area



A vehicle counts as having moved when it is tested in a different postcode area from the year before. That includes vehicles that changed garage without changing address. Moves are also counted only between two years in which the vehicle was observed, so a vehicle that disappears for a year and reappears elsewhere has no move recorded.








NoteTo be written



A short guide to reading each churn set, with an example question for each, written for readers who will not read the full churn report.

title: 13  How good is the data?
text:
13.1 Comparison with DfT vehicle counts
No administrative dataset is perfect, and this one combines three. This chapter summarises how far the CARS data can be relied on, mainly by comparing it with DfT’s official counts of vehicles. The pipeline’s data quality report (Data quality report, in the appendices) has every check in detail.
DfT’s vehicle licensing statistics count every vehicle on the DVLA register at the end of each year, licensed or SORN. The CARS data counts the vehicles observed (tested) in each year. The two should not agree exactly:
Figure 13.1: Vehicles aged three and over observed in the CARS data, as a ratio of DfT’s count of licensed and SORN vehicles of the same age, by body type.
For cars and vans aged three and over the two sources are close. CARS counts somewhat more cars than DfT (1.17 times as many in 2018, 1.04 in 2025), mainly because a car’s postcode area is carried forward for about two years after its last MOT, so recently scrapped cars are still counted. Counting vehicles of all ages, CARS falls below DfT in the most recent years, because vehicles first registered then have not yet been tested (Chapter 14).
Motorcycles are the exception: CARS observes a falling share of the motorcycles on DfT’s register, 0.55 of those aged three and over in 2025. Many motorcycles are kept on SORN or used seasonally, and so are tested irregularly.
Figure 13.2: Vehicles of all body types by age in 2022: observed in the CARS data and counted by DfT (licensed plus SORN).
By age (Figure 13.2), the sources agree well between about 3 and 16 years. Younger vehicles are missing from CARS because they have not had an MOT. Older vehicles are increasingly missing because many are kept on SORN, or are exempt from the MOT once 40 years old.

title: 13  How good is the data?
text:
13.3 Known issues

The final years are incomplete. 2025 is a partial year, and the youngest vehicles are missing from the last three years (Chapter 14).
Northern Ireland vehicles are included, but the test class is not supplied for them, and testing there was disrupted in 2020.
2005 appears to be of lower quality than later years, and some CARS reports start comparisons in 2006.
DVLA records describing another vehicle. Where a registration has moved between vehicles, the DVLA record may describe the wrong one. The pipeline detects the clear cases and does not use their values; some subtler cases will remain.
Make and model matching is very good for common vehicles and weaker for rare ones, motorcycles and specialist vehicles. model_confidence and model_method show how each match was made.







NoteTo be written



Quality of the linkage stage: match rates for the anonymised MOT data to the MOT history, and for the VES lookups; and the share of mileage judged implausible, by year.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.1 1. Observed is not the same as the fleet
This chapter collects, in one place, the things most likely to lead an analysis astray. Each is explained in more detail elsewhere in the book.
A vehicle is observed in a year when it has a postcode area in that year. That does not mean it was tested that year: the postcode area is copied back from a vehicle’s first MOT to its first registration, and carried forward for about two years after its last (Chapter 6). The observed vehicles are not the whole fleet: SORN vehicles, most heavy vehicles, most vehicles over 40 and, in the last three years, new vehicles not yet tested are missing (Chapter 1). For cars aged three to about sixteen, the observed count is close to DfT’s count of registered vehicles (Chapter 13).
What to do: say “vehicles observed” or “vehicles tested”, not “vehicles registered” or “the fleet”, and compare with DfT’s figures for ages three and over.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.2 2. The last three years are incomplete
text:
14.2 2. The last three years are incomplete
The number of vehicles observed peaks in 2019 and then falls (Figure 6.1). This is not a shrinking fleet. A new car has no location until its first MOT at three years old, so cars first registered in 2023 to 2025 are almost entirely missing, and the final year, 2025, is also only partly covered. In 2025 the CARS count of cars of all ages is 0.86 of DfT’s, against 1.1 in 2018.
What to do: for trends in the whole fleet, stop three years before the end of the data, or restrict to vehicles aged three and over. Never read a trend into the final year. Be especially careful with anything that is growing fast among new vehicles, such as electric cars, whose share is understated in recent years.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.3 3. Location is where the vehicle was tested
text:
14.3 3. Location is where the vehicle was tested
The postcode area is that of the MOT testing station (Chapter 7).
What to do: describe results as “vehicles tested in” an area. Do not treat a change of area as a change of address without saying so.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.4 4. Dead is not scrapped, and unknown is not missing at random
text:
14.4 4. Dead is not scrapped, and unknown is not missing at random
dead means “not tested since”, which includes vehicles scrapped, exported, on SORN or exempt. unknown covers new vehicles not yet tested and long gaps in a vehicle’s history (Chapter 6). Because a postcode area is carried forward for about two years after the last MOT, a vehicle only becomes dead some time after it stopped being tested.
What to do: call a vehicle that has become dead one that “stopped being tested”, not “scrapped”, unless you have other evidence. Remember that vehicles last seen in the final two years have not yet had the chance to become dead.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.5 5. Averages depend on who is in the denominator
text:
14.5 5. Averages depend on who is in the denominator
Average mileage is calculated over the vehicles with a (plausible) mileage that year, a group that changes from year to year and differs from the vehicles counted. Averages of averages are wrong (Chapter 12).
What to do: compute averages as total ÷ count over exactly the group you mean, and report the count alongside.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.6 6. Mileage needs a test at each end
text:
14.6 6. Mileage needs a test at each end
Annual mileage is shared out from the distance between two tests (Chapter 8). A year after a vehicle’s last test has no mileage; a long gap between tests spreads its distance across the gap, hiding any variation within it. 2020 is particularly affected by delayed tests.
What to do: compare years with similar coverage; be careful with year-on-year changes around 2020, and with vehicles near the start or end of their lives.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.7 7. Recorded, filled and assumed values
Many harmonised values were filled from similar vehicles or assumed from rules (Chapter 9). Most Euro statuses are assumed from dates; CO2, weight and type approval are often filled from similar vehicles.
What to do: check the _src column, and repeat key results using recorded values only. If the result changes, report both.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
section: 14.8 8. Plug-in hybrids are a lower bound
text:
14.8 8. Plug-in hybrids are a lower bound
Plug-in hybrids are identified from DfT’s records by model, and models sold both ways are left as ordinary hybrids (Chapter 4).
What to do: report plug-in hybrid numbers as “at least”, or combine all hybrids.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.9 9. Classifications differ between sources
MOT class 4 is not the same as DfT’s cars (Chapter 3).
What to do: use body_type when comparing with DfT, and state which classification you used.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.10 10. Postcode areas are big
Postcode areas average over very different places, and patterns between areas may not hold within them (Chapter 7).
What to do: use postcode area results for broad comparisons, not to describe neighbourhoods or individuals.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.11 11. Northern Ireland is different
Northern Ireland tests at four years in government test centres, its test class is not supplied, and its testing was disrupted in 2020. It is coded NI, a single area.
What to do: consider analysing Great Britain on its own, as the fleet profile tables do.

title: 14  Concepts and pitfalls
text:
14.12 12. Identifiers change between versions
vehicle_id is not stable between versions of the data (Chapter 10).
What to do: join on registration_DVSA, and record which version of the data you used.

title: 15  Getting started
text:
15.1 In a spreadsheet
This chapter explains how to open the CARS data in a spreadsheet and in code.
The aggregate tables are ordinary CSV files and open directly in Excel, LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets or Numbers.

title: 15  Getting started
text:
Size. Most tables are well under Excel’s limit of 1,048,576 rows. The largest, such as mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv, are several megabytes and open fine, but are easier to work with through a PivotTable.
Opening a CSV in Excel. Double-clicking a CSV works, but Excel may change values it thinks are dates or numbers. For full control use Data › From Text/CSV and check the column types in the preview.
Postcode area codes. Codes are one or two letters (B, LS). Excel will not change them, but take care with codes such as NA that some tools read as missing; no real postcode area uses it.
PivotTables (Insert › PivotTable) are the main tool for the examples in Chapter 16: they filter, group and sum the long tables.







TipExcel tables



Converting the data to an Excel table (select a cell, then Ctrl+T) makes filtering easier and lets formulas refer to columns by name.

title: 15  Getting started
text:
15.2 In code: DuckDB
The vehicle table is too large for a spreadsheet, and too large to load into memory in most tools, but DuckDB can query it in place. DuckDB is a free, fast database that runs inside R, Python or on its own, with no server to set up. It reads only the columns a query needs, so most queries on the vehicle table take seconds on an ordinary laptop.
The examples in this book are written in DuckDB’s SQL, so they work the same from any language. Each refers to the file as vehicles_enhanced.parquet; replace that with the path to your copy.

RPythonCommand line


install.packages("duckdb")

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())

dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC
")

dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
Packages such as dplyr (with duckplyr or dbplyr) and arrow can also query the file without writing SQL.


# pip install duckdb
import duckdb

duckdb.sql("""
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC
""").df()
polars and pandas (with pyarrow) can also read the file, but pandas loads everything into memory, so read only the columns you need.


# Install from https://duckdb.org/docs/installation/
duckdb -c "
  SELECT fuel_simple, count(*) AS n_vehicles
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  GROUP BY fuel_simple
  ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC"




Practical advice

Look before you query. DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet') lists the columns and their types instantly.
Select only the columns you need. SELECT * on the full table reads all of it. Name columns, or use DuckDB’s COLUMNS('^pca_') to pick a set by pattern.
Aggregate in DuckDB and bring back the result. Bring a summary into R or Python, not 93 million rows.
Memory. DuckDB uses up to 80% of memory by default and spills to disk when it needs more. For reshaping the whole table into long form, give it plenty of disk space (SET temp_directory = '...'), or work on a subset.
Try ideas on a subset. Filter to one make, one area or a random sample (USING SAMPLE 1%) while developing a query, then run it on everything.

title: 15  Getting started
text:
15.3 Hardware
Any recent laptop with 8 GB of memory and space for the 9 GB file can run the examples in this book. Reshaping the full table into one row per vehicle per year (about 2 billion rows) is better done on a machine with 32 GB or more, or broken into pieces.
