16.1 Example 1: average car mileage by postcode area
These examples use only the aggregate tables and a spreadsheet. The steps are written for Excel; other spreadsheets work the same way. The results shown were calculated from the same files, so you can check your answer against them.
Question: How far is the average car driven in each postcode area, and which areas have the highest and lowest mileage?
File: tables/mileage/mileage_by_pca_year_body_fuel.csv
Steps:
Result: the national average is 6,623 miles per car.
Interpreting it: low averages in London, and high ones in more rural areas, are what you would expect. 16.3 Example 3: the fleet by Euro standard
Question: How has the share of cars meeting each Euro standard changed?
File: tables/profile/a1_counts_cars.csv. This is a wide table: one row per year, and one column for each category of each characteristic, named characteristic: category.
Steps:

Open the file. Hide or delete the columns you don’t need, keeping year and the euro_standard: ... columns.
Add a column adding up the Euro standard columns for each year, and divide each column by it to get shares.
Select the year column and the share columns, and insert a line chart.









Figure 16.1: Share of cars by Euro standard, among cars with a plausible mileage in Great Britain. Most Euro standards are assumed from the date of manufacture (Chapter 4).





Interpreting it: the chart shows each standard rising as new cars meet it and falling as those cars age and leave the fleet. The profile tables count only cars with a plausible mileage that year, and exclude Northern Ireland.






ImportantSpotting a problem: Euro 6 cars in 2005



The chart shows 0.2% of cars as Euro 6 in 2005, nearly ten years before the standard existed. These are not real. They are cars whose Euro status was missing and was filled from similar vehicles (the same make, model, birth year and fuel), where a single wrong value recorded for one vehicle was copied to the rest of its group. The vehicle table flags them with euro_check = 'later_than_date'.
This is a good example of why you should check where values come from before relying on them. Most Euro standards in the data are filled or assumed rather than recorded; the euro_source: ... columns of the same table show how many of each. For a defensible analysis of Euro standards, use the vehicle table and exclude or correct values flagged later_than_date (Chapter 14, pitfall 7).

title: 17  Worked examples: code
text:
-- Vehicles observed in 2022, by body type and fuel group.
-- "Observed" means the vehicle has a real postcode area in 2022,
-- not one of the statuses unborn, dead or unknown.
SELECT
  body_type,
  fuel_simple,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles
FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
WHERE pca_2022 NOT IN ('unborn', 'dead', 'unknown')
GROUP BY body_type, fuel_simple
ORDER BY n_vehicles DESC;

title: 17  Worked examples: code
section: 17.2 Example 2: reshaping to one row per vehicle per year
text:
17.2 Example 2: reshaping to one row per vehicle per year
Question: How does the annual mileage of a Ford Fiesta change as it ages, and has that changed over time?
The vehicle table has one column per year. To analyse by age, the year columns need to become rows. DuckDB’s UNPIVOT does this: the mileage and plausibility columns are unpivoted separately and joined back together by vehicle and year. Filtering to one model first keeps the reshaped table small.
-- Average annual mileage of Ford Fiestas by age, for three years.
-- The vehicle table is wide (one column per year), so the mileage and
-- plausibility columns are first turned into long form: one row per
-- vehicle per year.
WITH fiesta AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  WHERE make_final = 'FORD' AND model_final = 'FIESTA'
),
mileage AS (
  UNPIVOT (SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^mileage_[0-9]{4}$') FROM fiesta)
  ON COLUMNS('^mileage_') INTO NAME col VALUE mileage
),
legit AS (
  UNPIVOT (SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^legit_mileage_[0-9]{4}$') FROM fiesta)
  ON COLUMNS('^legit_mileage_') INTO NAME col VALUE legit
)
SELECT
  CAST(right(m.col, 4) AS INTEGER) AS year,
  CAST(right(m.col, 4) AS INTEGER) - year(f.first_use_date) AS age,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles,
  round(avg(m.mileage)) AS mean_mileage,
  median(m.mileage) AS median_mileage
FROM mileage m
JOIN legit l
  ON l.vehicle_id = m.vehicle_id AND right(l.col, 4) = right(m.col, 4)
JOIN fiesta f ON f.vehicle_id = m.vehicle_id
WHERE l.legit                          -- plausible mileage only
  AND right(m.col, 4) IN ('2010', '2016', '2022')
GROUP BY year, age
HAVING age BETWEEN 3 AND 20
ORDER BY year, age;








Figure 17.1: Average annual mileage of Ford Fiestas by age, plausible mileage only.





Mileage falls with age, and the whole curve is lower in 2022 than in 2010. The query starts at age 3. A Fiesta has no odometer reading before its first MOT at three, so its mileage in earlier years can only come from sharing out the distance since new, and says little about use at each age.

17.3 Example 3: recorded against filled values
Question: Does the CO2 of new petrol and diesel cars depend on whether the value was recorded or filled from similar vehicles?
co2_src records where each harmonised value came from. Comparing the average of all values with the average of recorded values only is a quick test of whether filling gaps has changed a result.
-- CO2 of petrol and diesel cars first used 2012-2019: all values against
-- recorded values only. co2_src says where each value came from.
SELECT
  year(first_use_date) AS first_use_year,
  fuel_simple,
  count(co2) AS n_with_co2,
  round(avg(co2), 1) AS mean_co2_all,
  count(co2) FILTER (WHERE co2_src = 'dvla') AS n_recorded,
  round(avg(co2) FILTER (WHERE co2_src = 'dvla'), 1) AS mean_co2_recorded
FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
WHERE body_type = 'Cars'
  AND fuel_simple IN ('Petrol', 'Diesel')
  AND year(first_use_date) BETWEEN 2012 AND 2019
GROUP BY first_use_year, fuel_simple
ORDER BY fuel_simple, first_use_year;

title: 17  Worked examples: code
text:
17.4 Example 4: following a cohort
Question: What happened to the cars first used in 2008?
-- What happened to the cars first used in 2008? For each year, count how
-- many were observed, unknown or dead. Only the pca_YYYY columns are needed.
WITH cohort AS (
  SELECT vehicle_id, COLUMNS('^pca_[0-9]{4}$')
  FROM read_parquet('vehicles_enhanced.parquet')
  WHERE body_type = 'Cars' AND year(first_use_date) = 2008
),
long AS (
  UNPIVOT cohort ON COLUMNS('^pca_') INTO NAME col VALUE pca
)
SELECT
  CAST(right(col, 4) AS INTEGER) AS year,
  CASE WHEN pca IN ('unborn', 'dead', 'unknown') THEN pca
       ELSE 'observed' END AS status,
  count(*) AS n_vehicles
FROM long
GROUP BY year, status
ORDER BY year, status;








Figure 17.2: Cars first used in 2008, by their status in each year.





Almost the whole cohort is observed from 2008, although most cars had their first MOT only in 2011: once a car has been tested, its first postcode area is copied back to its first registration (Chapter 6). The cohort then gradually becomes dead as cars stop being tested, about two years after their last MOT, because the postcode area is carried forward. The few cars observed before 2008 have a first-use date later than their first record, such as imports or re-registered vehicles. The unknown line rises again at the end of the series: cars that may simply not have been tested yet (Chapter 14, pitfall 4).

22.1.1 Dates
Standerdised Birth/dead dates needed - Perhaps this should be moved to the linkage stage?

birth_date is the earliest of DVSA first used date, registration date and manufacture date. Only 10,030 input vehicles have none of these.
first_use_date is the first available of:

DVSA first used date
DVLA month of first registration
birth_date

first_use_source records which one was used.
last_mot_year is the latest year with is_end_use_YYYY = TRUE. Where no year is flagged, it is the last year with a recorded postcode area, unless that year is one of the final two years of data.



22.1.2 Postcode area status infill
The pca_YYYY variables thus far include the postcode area for each year a vehicle is observed. If the vehicle has not been observed in any given year the field is blank. At this stage blank values are infilled with an explanatory variable which descibes why the vehicle has not been observed, described below.



Condition (checked in order)
pca_YYYY becomes




A postcode area is recorded
the postcode area, unchanged


Birth year is the same as or later than year YYYY
unborn


The last MOT year (last_mot_year) is earlier than YYYY
dead


Otherwise
unknown



While these values are intended to make it easier to understanding the status of a vehicle in any given year, several important caveats must be under stood.

“Dead” means no longer observed, not necessarily scrapped. The data from the DVLA/DVSA does not provide a clear indication of when a vehicle stops being used. So we mark vehicle as dead after its last MOT. While most of these vehicles will have been scrapped, some will have been exported, or have been SORNed and not tested again. Some still be on the road an being driven illegally.
Unobserved years before the last MOT are “unknown”. Sometimes we loose track of a vehicle either because it did not have an MOT test in a particular year or because we could not match the DVSA MOT record to the anonymised MOT record. This means that we know the vehicle existed in that year and may have mileage associated with that vehicle, however we can’t give it a location. unknown vehicles increase substantially in the last few years due to vehicles that have not had their first MOT which we know exist from the DVLA / DVSA data but do not appear in the Anoymmised MOT dataset.



22.1.3 Scope: which vehicles are kept
The DVSA MOT dataset contains around 138 million vehicles, however many of these have no MOT history and were likely scrapped before the first digital MOT test records were created in 2005. Therfe for the CARS output tables aim to only include vehicles that have existed since the 1st of January 2005. As within the data there is no single way to confirm whether a vehicle exists we use four tests to define if the vehicle is in scope:








Flag
Rule

While most of these tests also mean that we have some data about the vehicles usage the DVLA activity flag can include vehicles that are over 40 years old and so no longer require a MOT test. While they are included in the output datasets we can say very little about how they are used and if or when they reached end of life.

22.2 Make and model cleaning
Code: R/make_model.R · Outputs: outputs/intermediate/dft_*.parquet, outputs/intermediate/make_model_*.parquet, outputs/quality/make_model_review.csv
Makes and models follow the naming of the DfT vehicle licensing statistics: tables VEH0220 (vehicles by make, generic model, model, fuel and engine size) and VEH0124 (by make, generic model, model and year of first use), which DfT builds from the DVLA register. Using the same names means MOT results can be joined to, and checked against, the official counts. No language model is used: every step is a rule, and every result records how it was reached.







Column
Meaning




make_final
DfT make, upper case (FORD, MERCEDES)


model_final
DfT generic model without the make (FIESTA, C CLASS, 1 SERIES)


dft_genmodel
The DfT GenModel (FORD FIESTA), for joins to DfT tables


dft_model
The DfT model string, when the raw model is exactly one


derivative_final
The rest of the raw model text: trim, engine, body style


body_type
DfT body type (Cars, Light goods vehicles, Motorcycles, …)


make_method, model_method, model_confidence, body_type_src
How each was found



Of 93,352,241 in-scope vehicles, 94.9% have a DfT generic model, 4.3% have a placeholder model such as UNKNOWN (so no model), and 0.8% keep their normalised raw model because nothing matched.

22.2.1 The DfT reference
inputs/df_VEH0220.csv and inputs/df_VEH0124_AM.csv / _NZ.csv are read as Latin-1 text. Each count is the number of vehicles (licensed plus SORN) at the end of a year, from 2014. To name models, each row is weighted by its largest count in any year, so a model that has since left the fleet still counts.
DfT’s coding has some quirks, which are tidied before matching:

Makes spelt two ways are merged. Makes differing only in punctuation or spaces (IVECO-FORD / IVECO FORD) join the larger. inputs/make_aliases.csv merges others: DfT files most Mercedes-Benz vehicles under MERCEDES, and uses MERCEDES-BENZ for recent registrations whose generic model is just the model text.
Generic models that are just a model string are recoded. Some recent registrations have a GenModel of the make plus the model string (HYUNDAI TUCSON ADVANCE PHEV AUTO). These model strings are matched like raw text against the rest of the make (TUCSON).
A long generic model name that extends a much more common one joins it, when it adds two or more words and has a tenth of the vehicles or fewer.
MODEL MISSING is no model.

Four reference tables come out of this (outputs/intermediate/dft_*.parquet): model names and body types, fuel group by engine band (used to settle ambiguous models, Section 22.2.4), year of first use, and the fuel as DfT records it, which is the only source that separates plug-in hybrids from other hybrids and is used in Section 22.3.5.

Text that starts with the make’s name (MINI COOPER) is also tried without it. Matches from the prefix, words and fuzzy steps must fit the vehicles’ MOT test class: motorcycles (classes 1 and 2) need a generic model that DfT mostly records as motorcycles, and other classes one it mostly does not. This stops HONDA S-WING 125 becoming the S800 car.
model_confidence is the share of the DfT vehicles under the matched text that have the chosen generic model: 1 for exact and generic, at least 0.9 for prefix and words.


22.2.4 Choices made per vehicle
For ambiguous and make_only text, each candidate generic model starts from its share of the DfT vehicles under the text. That share is multiplied by how common the vehicle’s fuel group and engine size band, and its year of first use, are among DfT vehicles of that generic model (with add-half smoothing, so a combination DfT never records is unlikely but possible). The candidate with the largest weight is chosen, and model_confidence is its share of the total weight. 936,073 vehicles are chosen this way, and 129,941 vehicles have a model_confidence below 0.5.
Engine size bands follow DfT: up to 50cc, 51–125cc, 126–200cc, then 100cc steps. Fuel groups are petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid (including plug-in and range extended), gas and other.


22.2.5 Derivative
derivative_final is the raw model text after the words that gave the make and model, kept as recorded apart from case and spacing. FIESTA ZETEC CLIMATE gives ZETEC CLIMATE; 118I M SPORT keeps all its words, because the badge is not part of the generic model name 1 SERIES. It is not standardised: it keeps the detail the DfT scheme drops (Discovery SPORT, C4 GRAND PICASSO) for analyses that need it. A derivative that only repeats the start of the model name (E for E CLASS) is dropped.


22.2.6 Body type
body_type uses the DfT body types. The first source that gives one wins (body_type_src):

The type approval mapping was checked against vehicles whose DfT model string has a single body type: 94% of N1 vehicles and over 99% of M1 and L3 vehicles agree.


22.2.7 Reviewed decisions and the review list

inputs/make_model_overrides.csv is applied last and wins over every step. Each row fixes one raw make/model spelling, gives the DfT make, generic model and derivative, and states the evidence. It is checked when read: a make is required, each raw pair may appear once, every row needs a reason, and a model must be a DfT generic model of the make. It has 15 rows. The first came from the fuel checks in Section 22.3.3, which caught an earlier lookup giving electric models to old petrol vehicles (PORSCHE TARGA as a Taycan).
inputs/make_aliases.csv merges make spellings (Section 22.2.1 and Section 22.2.2), with a reason for each.
outputs/quality/make_model_review.csv lists the raw pairs most worth reviewing, by vehicles: those matched by spelling fixes, word sets or vehicle attributes, or not matched at all, with the three nearest generic models of the make. Adding reviewed rows to the overrides file is how the matching improves.

Edit these files in R or a text editor. A spreadsheet re-saves numbers in its own format (45.160 becomes 45.16, 130E18 becomes 1.3E+020), which changes the raw keys.


22.2.8 Comparison with the DfT counts
R/dft_compare.R counts the in-scope vehicles observed in each year (a real PCA, not unborn, dead or unknown) by body type, age and make/model, and sets them against VEH0124’s licensed plus SORN counts (outputs/quality/dft_stock_*.csv). unknown is left out because it never ends for a vehicle with no last MOT year. Both sources cover the whole UK, Northern Ireland included. They differ by design: vehicles under three years old (four in Northern Ireland) have no MOT, and a SORN vehicle stays in DfT’s count but is not tested. The DfT scheme is the target. Its generic models are sometimes coarser than a buyer would use (DISCOVERY includes the Discovery Sport; ZX covers Kawasaki’s ZX-6R and ZX-10R) and sometimes finer (Lexus NX 300 and NX 450). The derivative keeps the raw detail.

text:
22.3 Stage 3: Record matching, fuel and engine checks, and backfill
Code: R/dvla_match.R, R/fuel_engine.R, R/euro_status.R, R/backfill.R (reference tables) and R/assemble.R (application) · Outputs: outputs/quality/dvla_make_aliases.csv, outputs/quality/suspected_dvla_mismatches.csv, outputs/intermediate/fuel_*.parquet, outputs/intermediate/backfill_*.parquet, then columns in the enhanced table
Eight attributes are harmonised: fuel, engine_cc, revenue_weight, co2, euro_status, type_approval, wheelplan and test_class. The stage runs in four steps:

Check whether each VES record describes the same vehicle (5.1).
Decide the fuel from the vehicle’s own records, then check it against its make/model (5.2, 5.3).
Set the engine size, with 0 for vehicles that have no engine (5.4).
Fill remaining gaps from vehicles with the same fuel (5.5, 5.6).

Figures below are for the 93,352,241 in-scope vehicles.

22.3.1 DVSA–DVLA record match
The DVSA and VES records of each vehicle are compared in three independent ways:







Comparison
Disagrees when




Make
The makes differ after removing punctuation, neither is a prefix of the other, and they do not share their first five characters. Known naming pairs (below) agree.


Year
Manufacture years differ by more than one year. Where either is missing, first registration years are compared instead.


Engine
Both engine sizes are recorded and differ by more than 100cc and by more than 10%.



A comparison that cannot be made counts as agreement. When at least two comparisons disagree, dvla_match is different: the VES record belongs to another vehicle, and none of its values (fuel, engine size, weight, CO2, Euro status, type approval, wheel plan) is used. dvla_evidence counts the disagreements.
Some make pairs are the same vehicle under another name: CHRYSLER-JEEP / JEEP, ROVER / AUSTIN, and motorhome converters such as FIAT / AUTO-TRAIL. They are found from the whole input file. A pair is an alias when it has at least 20 rows with comparable years (checks.dvla_alias_min_rows), and the years agree for at least 90% of them (checks.dvla_alias_min_year_agreement). This finds 392 pairs. The split is clear-cut:

Naming pairs agree on year 90–100% of the time.
Different makes, in pairs large enough to have qualified, agree 16.4% of the time. For example, BMW / AUDI agree 15.9% of the time.
Vehicles with the same make agree 99.90% of the time.

22.3.5 Plug-in hybrids: the DfT fuel detail
Neither source distinguishes a plug-in hybrid from any other hybrid. DVSA records Hybrid Electric (Clean) for a mild hybrid, a full hybrid and a plug-in alike, and Electric Diesel for both kinds of diesel hybrid; the VES fuel types map onto the same two labels. The DfT vehicle licensing statistics do distinguish them: table VEH0220, already read for the make/model naming scheme (Section 22.2.1), records eleven fuels, among them PLUG-IN HYBRID ELECTRIC (PETROL), PLUG-IN HYBRID ELECTRIC (DIESEL) and RANGE EXTENDED ELECTRIC.
VEH0220 counts vehicles rather than naming them, so the detail is attached by make and model (R/fuel_dft.R). Every DfT fuel and every harmonised fuel is put into the same set of narrow groups, and a vehicle is only ever matched against DfT rows in its own group:

The groups are what makes the replacement safe. A vehicle recorded as Electric can only match BATTERY ELECTRIC, so it can never become a hybrid; a petrol vehicle can only match PETROL, so it can never pick up a diesel fuel; and a petrol hybrid can only become one of the three petrol hybrid fuels. A range extender sits with the petrol hybrids, not with battery electric, because it has a petrol engine and DVSA records those vehicles as hybrids. Other and Steam have no DfT counterpart and are matched in no group at all.
Within its group a vehicle takes the most common DfT fuel for:

its DfT model string (fuel_DFT_src = dft_model), the value of dft_model from Section 22.2.3
its generic model (dft_genmodel), when the raw model text gave no DfT model string

A level is used only when one DfT fuel holds at least 0.9 of that level’s DfT vehicles in the group. Otherwise the vehicle is left unmatched and recorded as ambiguous_model or ambiguous_genmodel.
That threshold is the answer to models sold both as a plug-in and not. Model strings are nearly always clear-cut, because the string names the variant: “NIRO 3 PHEV S-A” against “NIRO 3 HEV S-A”, “X1 XDRIVE25E M SPORT AUTO” against “X1 SDRIVE 20I M SPORT MHEV A”, “XC40 + T4 RECHARGE AUTO” against “XC40 + B4 MHEV AUTO”. Of the DfT model strings that carry a petrol hybrid, 3,125 of 3,126 have one fuel above the threshold (measured once against the full build, as are the model shares below). Generic models often are not clear-cut: BMW X1 petrol hybrids are 56% mild hybrid and 44% plug-in, and KIA NIRO petrol hybrids 84% full hybrid and 16% plug-in, so an X1 or a NIRO whose model text gave no model string is left unmatched rather than guessed at. HYUNDAI KONA shows the other case: it is sold as petrol, battery electric and full hybrid but has never been sold as a plug-in, so its petrol hybrids are unambiguous at generic-model level and are matched.

The harmonised fuel is then replaced only for the three plug-in fuels, and only when the vehicle has an engine size above 0: a plug-in hybrid has both an engine and a plug, so a “plug-in hybrid” with no engine contradicts itself and keeps its recorded fuel. fuel_src becomes dft where the replacement was made.

What this does not do. The DfT fuel is a property of the make, model and variant, not of the individual vehicle, so a vehicle whose model text was matched to the wrong model string takes the wrong fuel with it. The match is only as good as Section 22.2, and model_confidence is the guide to that. Nor can it find a plug-in hybrid whose make/model DfT does not record at all (no_reference), or one of an ambiguous generic model: those vehicles are undercounted as ordinary hybrids, which makes 1,090,074 a lower bound on the plug-in fleet.

The recorded Euro status is standardised first (R/euro_status.R), because VES writes one status in many ways: “EURO 6 AP”, “EURO 6AP”, “EURO6AP” and “EURO 6 (AP)” all become “EURO 6 AP”. Case, spacing and punctuation are made consistent, “+” is written as PLUS, clear typing errors are fixed (V1 for VI, 1SC or 15C for ISC, 0BD for OBD), and repeats of the standard are dropped (“EURO 6 EURO 6 AP”, “EURO 5 (FIVE)”, “EURO VI E (6)”). Nothing else is removed, and euroStatus_DVLA keeps the value as supplied. The value is written as EURO, the standard, then the remaining letters and digits, with hyphens around the words TEMP, EVAP, ISC, FCM, BIS, OBD, WLTP and PLUS (“EURO 6 D-TEMP-EVAP-ISC”, “EURO VI OBD-E”). Spaces are kept only between two numbers (“EURO VI 66D0”, “EURO 5 134 2014”).
Each takes the first available of:

the recorded value (*_src = dvla or dvsa)
the most common value for the same make, model, birth year, fuel and engine size (variant). The engine size is the vehicle’s engine_cc from 5.4, so it may itself be backfilled, and electric vehicles match other electric vehicles at 0.
the most common value for the same make, model, birth year and fuel (model_year_fuel)
for euro_status only, the standard that was compulsory for new registrations when the vehicle was made (euro_schedule, Section 22.3.7)
otherwise missing (*_src empty)

For vehicles with a mismatched VES record, recorded VES values are ignored and filled as if missing. This affects the CO2 value of 115,761 vehicles.
A recorded CO2 of 0 g/km is only kept for a vehicle with no engine. Only a pure electric or fuel cell vehicle can emit nothing; anywhere else a zero is a value the VES never held, and taken at face value it would put millions of petrol cars and diesel vans in the “0 g/km” band. The zero is cleared in R/fuel_engine.R, before the backfill references are built, so that the modal CO2 of a variant is taken from real values only and a vehicle recorded as 0 is filled from similar vehicles instead. A vehicle with no fuel recorded is not known to be electric, so its zero goes too. co2Emissions_DVLA keeps the value as supplied, and co2_check records what happened:

22.3.7 Euro status from the registration date
A Euro status is recorded for only a minority of vehicles. The VES returns one mostly for vehicles first registered from 2018 onwards, so after the variant backfill of Section 22.3.6 44.6% of in-scope vehicles still had none.
The standards were phased in on fixed dates, though, and a vehicle cannot have been registered new in Great Britain after the date a standard became compulsory without meeting it. So where nothing else says otherwise, a missing Euro status takes the standard in force when the vehicle was made (R/euro_status.R, euro_status_src = euro_schedule).
Three decisions make that assumption as weak as the rules allow:

The compulsory dates, not the type-approval dates. Each standard opened for new type approvals a year or more before it became compulsory for all new registrations. Using the later date means a vehicle may well meet a newer standard than it is given here, but it cannot meet an older one.
The date the vehicle was made, not its British registration date. birth_date is the earliest of the DVSA first-used, registration and manufacture dates (Section 22.1.1), which for an import is the manufacture date rather than the later British first registration. Tested against the 11.3 million vehicles whose birth_date is more than a year before their first_use_date, birth_date errs towards an older standard and first_use_date towards a newer one, so birth_date is used (first_use_date only where birth_date is missing).

The percentages in the rest of this section were measured once, against the full build, by comparing the schedule with the vehicles that do have a recorded Euro status; they are a record of that check and are not recomputed here. - One schedule per vehicle class. Vans were a year or two behind cars, lorries and buses ran on the heavy-duty timetable, and motorcycles reached Euro 4 only in 2017. Applying the car dates to motorcycles would be too new for 99.98% of the motorcycles that do have a recorded status.

Only recorded values are counted, plus the 0 engine size given to vehicles with no engine. Backfilled values are never fed back into the tables.
Ties go to the lowest value (the smallest number, or alphabetically first for text), so results are the same on every run.
A group’s value is used only if at least backfill.min_vehicles vehicles had it recorded. The setting is 1.
Vehicles without a make, model or fuel contribute to no table and receive no backfilled values. Vehicles without a birth year are used only for the model-fuel table.



22.3.9 Assumptions and limitations

Two disagreements between DVSA and VES mean different vehicles. One disagreement is common for genuine matches: imports registered years after manufacture, and engine sizes recorded differently. A registration moved between two vehicles of the same make and year, where one engine size is missing, is not detected; the fuel check catches some of these.
DVSA fuel is trusted unless another record contradicts it. VES overrides it only for “Other”, and for Electric / Fuel Cells vehicles that VES shows as hybrids or as having an engine.
A recorded engine size on an Electric vehicle is evidence of an engine, unless VES confirms it is electric (for example a converted classic that keeps its original engine size on record), or the make/model is electric-only.
Vehicles with no engine have engine size 0. Range-extender and hybrid vehicles recorded as Electric by both DVSA and VES, with no engine size, get



Rare fuels are flagged, not corrected. LPG conversions, electric conversions of classic cars and uncommon factory variants are all legitimate, so only electric-only models, where the records disagree, are corrected.
The fuel check depends on the make/model cleaning. Merged or wrong models produce rare_for_model and implausible_for_model flags; these point to raw spellings worth reviewing. Small make/models (under 100 vehicles) are not checked, and on the 1% sample most make/models are no_reference.
A model’s DfT fuel is its vehicles’ fuel. The plug-in distinction of Section 22.3.5 is a property of the model string, not of the individual vehicle, so it is only as good as the make/model match and cannot find a plug-in hybrid of a model DfT records both ways. The plug-in counts are a lower bound.
A vehicle registered new after a standard became compulsory meets it. The Euro status of Section 22.3.7 is an assumption about the rules, not an observation of the vehicle. It is wrong for used imports and rebuilt vehicles, which take a British registration long after they were built; birth_date limits that, and euro_status_src separates assumed values from recorded ones so they can be dropped.
Vehicles of the same make, model, birth year and fuel share attributes. This is reasonable for wheel plan, type approval and test class. It is weaker for CO2 and weight, which vary with trim, gearbox and body style.
Birth year stands in for model year.
At the variant level, engine size must match to the cc. Near-identical engines (1596 cc vs 1598 cc) form separate groups; the model-year-fuel level then applies.
A vehicle with a backfilled engine size matches the most common variant of its make, model, year and fuel, and takes that variant’s attributes.
A single recorded vehicle is enough to fill a group. This follows from min_vehicles = 1.
Missing values are not random. VES values are mostly missing where no VES record was found, which is more common for older and scrapped vehicles. Their gaps are filled from vehicles that do have records.
“Other” is treated as one fuel group, although it covers a mix of fuels.
Euro status spellings are standardised, not interpreted (5.6). The letters after the standard are kept together, because the stage letter and the emission code cannot be told apart once the spacing varies: “EURO 6D AR” and “EURO 6 DAR” are both “EURO 6 DAR”, and stay separate from “EURO 6 AR”. Other misspellings still count as separate values. The derived euro_standard column (Section 22.4.1) is more robust.

For analysis sensitive to these assumptions, filter to recorded values with *_src IN ('dvsa', 'dvla'), or to fuel_check = 'ok'. The churn tables use the recorded DVSA fuel, engine size and test class columns by default.

22.4.2 Number plate decoding
The registration is upper-cased and stripped of non-alphanumeric characters (registration_clean). It is then matched against a sequence of plate formats, and the first match wins. The rules are an SQL translation of DVLAAPI::registration_analysis(), in the same order. The main formats are:

The plate period gives plate_date, plate_date_from (first day of the first month) and plate_date_to (first day of the last month).
vanity_plate is TRUE when birth_date falls outside the plate period, widened by 30 days (plates.vanity_tolerance_days) at each end.
vanity_plate is missing when the plate has no dated period, or the vehicle has no birth date.

Assumptions and limitations:

The DVSA registration is the plate the vehicle carries.
The rules are simple pattern checks. They follow the DVLAAPI package and should be read as indicative, not definitive.

imported vehicles registered years after manufacture
Q plates
re-registered vehicles

The period end is the first day of the last month, so the 30-day tolerance partly serves to cover the rest of that month.

title: Data dictionary
text:
Reading the coverage sections
This part describes every column of the vehicle table. The pipeline writes the table in two versions:
This part describes the maximal table, and the Simplified column of each chapter’s table says whether a column is also in the simplified table. A column has the same name, type and values in both. The columns are grouped by theme, one chapter per group, and each chapter has the same three sections:
The descriptions and missing shares come from the pipeline’s data_dictionary.csv, so they always match the version of the data the book describes. Missing is the share of the 93,352,241 vehicles with no value. The year-by-year columns (mileage_YYYY, legit_mileage_YYYY and pca_YYYY) are listed once each, with the range of their missing shares across the years.
A column’s coverage is the share of vehicles with a value in it, that is, not blank. Coverage depends a great deal on the age of the vehicle, because the sources describe vehicles differently according to when they were on the road: the DVLA Vehicle Enquiry Service was queried between 2024 and 2026, so it rarely holds a record for a vehicle scrapped long before (8  Source data and linkage). The coverage sections therefore show each column by year of first use (first_use_date), with the vehicles of that year as the denominator.
The year-by-year columns are different: they describe a calendar year, so their coverage is shown for each year, among the vehicles on the road in that year (those whose pca_YYYY is not unborn or dead).
Two things to keep in mind:
The coverage figures were counted from the vehicle table by scripts/run-coverage.R (run 2026-10-21 20:01), and the values by scripts/run-values.R.

title: Data dictionary
text:
A value is not necessarily a recorded value. Many harmonised columns are filled from similar vehicles where the sources are blank. The _src column next to each says which values were recorded and which were filled (14  Concepts and pitfalls).
Some values mean “not known”. A column that is never blank can still hold unknown, no_reference or missing, as pca_YYYY and the _check columns do. The overview of each chapter says where this applies.

registration_DVSA is the plate as supplied in the DVSA MOT history. It is the plate the vehicle carried when the data was extracted, which may not be the one it was first registered with.
registration_DVLA is the plate returned by the DVLA Vehicle Enquiry Service (VES) for this vehicle. It usually matches the DVSA plate; where it does not, the plate has moved to another vehicle, and dvla_match

says whether the VES record can be trusted.

registration_clean is the DVSA plate upper-cased with spaces and punctuation removed. Use it for joins.
registration_at_first_test is the plate the vehicle carried at its first MOT test, as recorded by DVSA. It differs from registration_DVSA where the plate has changed since, for example to a cherished plate. The pipeline carries it through without using it.
The plate_ columns decode the plate’s format: its type (current style, prefix, suffix, dateless and others), the period in which a plate of that form was issued, and the issuing office or region.
vanity_plate is TRUE where the vehicle’s birth date falls outside the plate’s issue period. This flags cherished plates, but also imports, Q plates and other re-registered vehicles.
plate_ever_changed_VES is TRUE where the registration returned a different vehicle between VES lookups.








ImportantRegistrations are personal data



Registration marks can identify a vehicle’s keeper when combined with other information. The conditions for using them are set out in Chapter 10.

The DVSA registration, and everything decoded from it, is present for every vehicle. The plate’s issue dates are blank only for the 76,240 vehicles whose plate has no dated period, and vanity_plate is blank where either the plate period or the birth date is missing.

title: 26  Vehicle type
text:
body_type is the DfT body type: Cars, Light goods vehicles, Motorcycles, Buses and coaches, Heavy goods vehicles or Other vehicles. It is the usual way to select, for example, cars only. body_type_src records whether it came from the DfT model, the DVLA type approval, the generic model or the MOT test class (methodology, section 4.6).
test_class is the MOT test class (1 to 7) and type_approval the European type approval category (M1, N1, L3 and so on). Both take the recorded value where there is one (test_class_ANON and the DVLA type approval), and otherwise the most common value among similar vehicles that share the other one, first of the same make, model, birth year, fuel and engine size, then of the same make, model, birth year and fuel. A borrowed value that contradicts the other classifications, the wheel plan or the engine size is not used. Each has a _src column saying which (methodology, section 5.6).
The supplied columns (_DVLA, _ANON) are the values as received, including the DVLA flag for automated vehicles, which the pipeline does not use.

text:
26.2 Coverage
body_type is present for 97% of vehicles and changes little with age (Figure 26.1). The vehicles without one are those whose model could not be matched and which have no type approval or test class to fall back on.

type_approval is rare for vehicles first used before 2000 (26%), because the DVLA rarely records a type approval category for them, and the backfill can only copy values that similar vehicles have. From the mid-2000s it is present for more than 90%.
test_class comes from the anonymised MOT data, so it is present only for vehicles that have been tested, or are like vehicles that have. Coverage falls for vehicles first used since 2023, which are too new for their first MOT test: 78% for 2025.

typeApproval_DVLA shares the pattern of every VES field, being present only where a VES record was found (Chapter 36). automatedVehicle_DVLA is present only for some vehicles first used since 2021 (25% of those first used in 2025).

27.1 Overview
Both the DVSA and DVLA sources record the vehicle’s colour, but in different ways. The CARS pipeline keeps the values as supplied and does not modify them.
Vehicles can change colour over time (although most don’t). The DVSA do not provide a record of colour changes over time so the primaryColour_DVSA and secondaryColour_DVSA are likely to be the most recent values. The DVLA VES API also does not provide a record of colour changes over time, but repeted quering of the API may have found some vehicles that have changed colour. However in the main CARS ouputs only the most recent colour is kept.

title: 28  Wheel plan
text:
28.1 Overview

title: 30  Fuel and engine
text:
fuel is the harmonised fuel, in DVSA’s terms. It is the DVSA value, replaced by the DVLA value where DVSA says Other or the two clearly disagree, and checked against the fuel of other vehicles of the same make and model (methodology, section 5.2 and section 5.3). fuel_src says where it came from and fuel_check how it compares with the make and model.
fuel_DFT is the fuel DfT’s licensing statistics record for the vehicle’s model, which unlike DVSA and DVLA separates plug-in hybrids. It is how plug-in hybrids are identified (section 5.5).
fuel_simple groups the harmonised fuel into six categories: Petrol, Diesel, Electric, Hybrid Electric, Plug-in Hybrid Electric and Other (section 6.1). It is the column most analyses need.
engine_cc is the engine size in cc: DVSA, else DVLA, else the most common for similar vehicles, and 0 for electric and fuel cell vehicles (section 5.4). engine_cc_src and engine_check record where it came from and what was corrected.
fuel_DVSA, fuelType_DVLA, engineSize_DVSA and engineCapacity_DVLA are the values as supplied.







ImportantPlug-in hybrids are a lower bound



A vehicle is a plug-in hybrid in fuel_simple only when its DfT model is clearly one. Models sold as both plug-in and ordinary hybrids stay as ordinary hybrids, so plug-in hybrids are undercounted (Chapter 14).

title: 30  Fuel and engine
text:
30.2 Coverage
The harmonised fuel is never blank: fuel_DVSA is supplied for every vehicle, and 98.5% of harmonised values are the DVSA value unchanged. A fuel of Other or a fuel_check of unknown_fuel or no_reference means the fuel is not really known, or could not be checked.
fuel_DFT is present for 94% of vehicles, those whose model is found in the DfT statistics with a fuel of the same group. It is lower for the oldest vehicles (90% of those first used before 2000), as for the model match itself (Chapter 25).
The engine size shows most clearly why the harmonised columns are worth using (Figure 30.1). The DVSA engine size comes from the MOT history, so it is missing for vehicles that have not yet been tested: only 1% of vehicles first used in 2024 have one. The DVLA engine capacity fills most of these, but is itself missing for older vehicles with no VES record. Combining them, and filling the rest from similar vehicles, gives engine_cc for 99.1% of vehicles, at every age.

title: 31  Emissions
text:
co2 is the official CO2 figure in g/km, measured when the model was type approved. It is the DVLA value where the VES record describes this vehicle, or else the most common value among vehicles of the same make, model, birth year, fuel and engine size, and failing that of the same make, model, birth year and fuel. A recorded 0 g/km is kept only for vehicles with no engine; anywhere else it is cleared and filled from similar vehicles. co2_src and co2_check record what was done (methodology, section 5.6).
euro_status is the Euro standard as text (EURO 6 AP), standardised from the DVLA’s many spellings, backfilled from similar vehicles, and otherwise assumed to be the standard compulsory for new vehicles of that type when the vehicle was made (section 5.7). euro_standard is its number (1 to 6), and euro_status_src and euro_check record where it came from and whether it fits the vehicle’s age.
co2Emissions_DVLA, euroStatus_DVLA and realDrivingEmissions_DVLA are the values as supplied.







ImportantRecorded, filled and assumed values



Filled and assumed values are estimates, not records. Results that depend on CO2 or Euro standard should be checked using only the recorded values (co2_src = 'dvla', euro_status_src = 'dvla'): Chapter 17 shows how, and Chapter 14 explains why.

title: 31  Emissions
text:
31.2 Coverage
CO2 has been recorded since vehicle tax began to depend on it, for cars registered from March 2001, so the DVLA figure is almost never present for vehicles first used before then (Figure 31.1). The backfill cannot help here, as similar vehicles of the same age have no figure either: co2 is present for only 9% of vehicles first used before 2000, against 93% of those first used in the 2010s. The DVLA figure dips again for the newest vehicles, not yet looked up in the VES (Chapter 36), and the backfill fills most of that gap.
The DVLA recorded a Euro status for only 15% of vehicles, almost all first used since 2018. The backfill and the assumed standard raise this to 91% with a standard (euro_standard), but most of the values are therefore not records. For cars, 59% of Euro statuses are assumed from the date. euro_status is never blank: where no standard applies it says why instead, pre_euro for vehicles made before the first standard of their class (in 1992 for cars), no_schedule for body types with no Euro schedule and no_date where the vehicle has no date to place it. euro_standard is blank for these.
realDrivingEmissions_DVLA, the DVLA’s Real Driving Emissions (RDE) field, is present only for some vehicles first used since 2019, and is not used by the pipeline.

32.1 Overview
These columns attach to each car the size, mass and official emissions of its model, from the RACF car fleet. That fleet is DfT’s car fleet by make, model, year of first use and fuel, enriched with each model’s SMMT segment (supermini, SUV and so on; Chapter 3) and with its mass, dimensions, CO2, energy use and electric range from the EU type-approval and Dutch RDW registers. It holds counts and model attributes only, not vehicle records.
Each value is the fleet-weighted mean over the linked RACF rows with a plausible value, so it describes the model, not the individual car. How the link is made is set out in the methodology, section 6 and section 9.3.
racf_link_level, racf_suv_share and racf_eu_exact_share are in the maximal table only. The SMMT segment and the size, mass, CO2 and energy columns are also in the simplified table.

title: 32  Car size and model attributes
text:
racf_link_level says how the car was linked to the RACF fleet:

model: the same make, DfT generic model and model string, year of first use and fuel group;
genmodel: failing that, the same make, generic model, year and fuel group, averaging over the generic model’s model strings;
none: not linked.

Only cars (body_type Cars) are linked, so the column and every racf_ column is blank for other vehicles.
racf_smmt_type is the SMMT segment with the largest fleet among the linked RACF rows, and racf_suv_share the share of that fleet the SMMT calls a crossover / SUV or an off-roader.
The size and mass columns are the EU mass in running order (racf_mass_kg), the RDW kerb weight, length, width and height, the wheelbase, and the footprint (wheelbase times track, in m²).
The emissions and energy columns are the EU NEDC and WLTP CO2 figures in g/km, the energy use in Wh/km and the electric range in km.
racf_eu_exact_share is the share of the linked RACF fleet matched to the EU type-approval data for its exact year. The rest borrows another year’s or fuel’s values.








ImportantModel values, not measurements



A car’s racf_co2_nedc is the average for its model, year and fuel, not its own figure, which is in co2 (Chapter 31). The racf_ columns are best used to describe groups of cars, such as the fleet’s average size or the share of SUVs, and for cars with racf_eu_exact_share well below 1 they are borrowed from another year or fuel.

32.2 Coverage
racf_link_level is present for the 81% of vehicles that are cars. Most of those link to a model, so racf_smmt_type is present for 74% of all vehicles. The other columns are present only where the linked RACF rows have a plausible value, and their coverage follows the registers they come from (Figure 32.1):

The EU mass and footprint and the RDW kerb weight are present for most cars: racf_mass_kg for 74% of all vehicles. The RDW width and length are present for fewer.
NEDC CO2 applies to cars approved before the WLTP test replaced it, so racf_co2_nedc is present for most cars first used up to 2020 and racf_co2_wltp for most of those first used from 2018 (62% of vehicles first used in 2022). Cars first used from 2018 to 2020 often have both.
Energy use and electric range apply only to plug-in cars, so they are present for 5.5% of vehicles, rising for the newest.

title: 33  Dates and age
text:
33.1 Overview
A vehicle has several dates that mark the start of its life: when it was made, when it was first registered, and when it was first used on the road. For most vehicles these are within weeks of each other, but they can be years apart for an import or a vehicle that sat in stock. Chapter 6 describes the stages of a vehicle’s life and how the data records them.
How these dates are built is set out in the methodology, section 3.2, and how the last MOT test date is read in section 3.5. Other DVLA dates, such as tax due and MOT expiry, are described with the licensing status in Chapter 36.

title: 33  Dates and age
text:
first_use_date is the date to use for a vehicle’s age: the DVSA first used date, else the DVLA month of first registration, else birth_date. first_use_source records which.
birth_date is the earliest of the DVSA first used, registration and manufacture dates; for the few vehicles with none of these, it is taken from the DVLA dates, and birth_date_source records which. It decides when a vehicle is unborn in pca_YYYY (Chapter 35).
final_test_date_DVSA is the date of the last recorded MOT test, and last_mot_year the year after which the vehicle is treated as dead: no longer observed, not necessarily scrapped (Chapter 14). last_mot_year is the last year in which is_end_use_YYYY is TRUE (Chapter 35).
The MOT test dates as supplied are carried through unchanged: first_test_date_DVSA and first_test_year_DVSA for the first test, final_test_year_DVSA for the last, and lastMotTestDate_DVSA. Use final_test_date_DVSA rather than lastMotTestDate_DVSA: DVSA put a date in the future in lastMotTestDate_DVSA for vehicles that have never been tested.
The supplied dates (_DVSA, _DVLA) are kept as received. The DVLA month of first registration is accurate to the month only.

title: 33  Dates and age
text:
33.2 Coverage
Because three sources are combined, first_use_date and birth_date are missing for almost no vehicles. 82% of first use dates are the DVSA first used date, 14% the DVLA month of first registration and 4% the birth date. A few dates are implausible: 123 vehicles have a first use date before 1900 or after 2026.
The coverage of the supplied dates follows their sources (Figure 33.1):

The DVSA first used date and last test date come from the MOT history, so they are present for tested vehicles only. Coverage falls sharply for vehicles first used since 2023, most of which have not had their first MOT: 38% for 2023 and 1% for 2024. The DVSA registration and manufacture dates are present for almost every vehicle.
The DVLA dates are present wherever a VES record was found (Chapter 36). monthOfFirstDvlaRegistration_DVLA is different: it is present only for the 1.0% of vehicles first registered somewhere else, such as imports.
The supplied first and final test dates (first_test_date_DVSA, first_test_year_DVSA and final_test_year_DVSA) are present for 84% of vehicles, those that have had an MOT test. lastMotTestDate_DVSA is present for more, 94%, because it also holds the future dates of untested vehicles.
last_mot_year is blank by design for a vehicle that is still being tested, or that was last seen in the final two years of data. Its coverage is therefore highest for old vehicles, most of which have left the road, and close to zero for new ones.

title: 34  Mileage
text:
34.1 Overview
The MOT test records the odometer reading, and the difference between two tests gives the distance driven between them. The annualisation spreads that distance over the calendar years between the tests to give an annual mileage for each year. Chapter 8 explains how the annual figures are made, and Chapter 1 what the MOT records.
The pipeline takes the annual mileages as supplied (methodology, section 2), and summarises them in the mileage tables (section 8; Chapter 12). The table is wide, with one mileage column per year: Chapter 17 shows how to reshape it to one row per vehicle per year.

title: 34  Mileage
text:
mileage_YYYY is the number of miles driven in year YYYY, from 2005 to 2025.
legit_mileage_YYYY is TRUE if that mileage is judged plausible. Filter on it for most analyses: the implausible values include odometer errors and readings typed in wrongly.
total_mileage is the sum of the annual mileages over all years. It is 0 for a vehicle with no recorded mileage, and decides scope_mileage (Chapter 23).
odometer_est_YYYY is the annualisation’s estimate of the odometer reading in year YYYY, carried through unchanged. The pipeline does not use it: some estimates exceed 1,000,000 miles and some fall from one year to the next. It is in the maximal table only.








ImportantMileage needs a test at each end



An annual mileage can only be calculated between two MOT tests, so a vehicle has none before its first test or after its last, and the most recent years are incomplete because many vehicles have not yet had their next test (Chapter 14).

title: 34  Mileage
text:
34.2 Coverage
The mileage columns are blank for most vehicles in most years (Table 34.1), simply because a vehicle is on the road for only part of the period. A fairer measure is the share of the vehicles on the road in a year, that is with a pca_YYYY that is not unborn or dead, that have a mileage for that year (Figure 34.1).
On that measure about 76% of vehicles on the road have a mileage in each year from 2010 to 2023. The rest are mostly vehicles not yet due their first MOT, and vehicles in the years after their last test whose status is still unknown. Coverage is higher in the first years (87% in 2005) and falls in the last two, to 72% in 2024 and 50% in 2025, because many vehicles have not yet had the test that closes the year.
Of the mileages present, almost all are judged plausible: the share flagged implausible is at most 1.7% in any year. total_mileage is never blank, but is 0 for vehicles with no mileage in any year.
odometer_est_YYYY is present in each year for as many vehicles as have a plausible mileage (76% of those on the road in 2015), so it adds no years that mileage_YYYY does not already cover.

title: 35  Location and yearly status
text:
35.1 Overview
The only location in the data is the postcode area of the testing station where the vehicle had its MOT test in each year: LS for Leeds, B for Birmingham, and so on. It is where the vehicle was tested, which is usually, but not always, near where it is kept. Chapter 7 explains postcode areas and the limits of analysing vehicles at this scale.
The status rules are set out in the methodology, section 3.3, and how the statuses describe a vehicle’s life in Chapter 6. A vehicle is observed in a year when pca_YYYY holds a real postcode area, and selecting these vehicles is the usual first step of any analysis of a year (Chapter 11).

title: 35  Location and yearly status
text:
pca_YYYY is the postcode area in year YYYY, from 2005 to 2025. Northern Ireland is coded BT, its real postcode area (older deliveries’ NI is recoded to BT).
In a year with no recorded postcode area, the pipeline replaces the blank with the vehicle’s status:

unborn: the vehicle had not yet been made or registered;
dead: the year is after the vehicle’s last MOT test, so it is no longer observed. This is not the same as scrapped: it includes vehicles exported, declared off the road or simply no longer tested;
unknown: the vehicle existed but was not observed, for example in its first three years before the first MOT.





is_new_vehicle_YYYY is the new-vehicle flag for the year, and is_intertest_YYYY its inter-test flag. The pipeline does not use them.
is_end_use_YYYY is TRUE in the year of the vehicle’s final MOT test, and only where testing has stopped. The last year in which it is TRUE gives last_mot_year (Chapter 33), and so the years in which pca_YYYY is dead.

title: 36  Licensing status and DVLA lookups
text:
Licensing status: tax status and due date, MOT status and expiry, whether the vehicle is marked for export, the date of its latest V5C (registration certificate) and the end date of the additional rate of tax (the supplement for cars with a high list price), all as at the last lookup that returned a record. These are supplied by the DVLA and not changed. Chapter 6 explains SORN, export and the other stages they describe.
What changed between lookups: ever_SORN, ever_export_marked, plate_ever_changed_VES, v5C_issue_date_ever_changed and change_in_other_VES_field summarise the changes seen across repeated lookups.
The lookups: when the registration was first and last queried and first and last returned a record, how many queries were made, and the error from the last one where it failed (methodology, section 2). n_DVLA_makes is the number of different makes the lookups returned: more than one suggests the plate moved between vehicles.
dvla_match says whether the VES record describes the same vehicle as the DVSA record. A registration can move between vehicles, so a lookup can return another vehicle’s record. Where at least two of make, year of manufacture and engine size disagree (dvla_evidence), the match is different and the pipeline does not use the record’s values (section 5.1).

title: 36  Licensing status and DVLA lookups
text:
36.2 Coverage
These columns have three levels of coverage, which apply to every _DVLA column in the table:

A lookup was made: 97% of vehicles. The lookup columns, such as first_VES_check and is_error, are present for all of these.
The lookup returned a record: 77% of vehicles. The licensing status columns and the other _DVLA columns are present only for these.
The record describes this vehicle: dvla_match is same for 77% of vehicles, different for 0.1% and no_dvla for the rest.

How often a record was returned depends strongly on age (Figure 36.1). The VES only describes vehicles still on the DVLA register, so it returned a record for 62% of vehicles first used before 2000 and 65% of those first used in the 2000s, most of which have long left the road, against 96% of those first used in the 2010s. Where no record was returned, error holds the reason.
Vehicles first used in the last few years are a different case: many had not been registered, or had not reached the DVSA data, when the lookups were made. Hardly any vehicle first used in 2026 has a DVLA record (1%).
Some status fields are blank even where a record was returned, because the DVLA holds no value: taxDueDate_DVLA for some vehicles that are not taxed, motExpiryDate_DVLA for vehicles too new to need an MOT, and artEndDate_DVLA for all but the recent, expensive cars that pay the additional rate of tax.

title: Appendix A — Glossary
text:
Annualisation

Converting each vehicle’s test history into one figure per calendar year (Chapter 8).

Backfill

Filling a missing attribute with the most common value among similar vehicles: the same make, model, birth year and fuel (Chapter 9).

Birth date

In CARS, the earliest of a vehicle’s first-use, registration and manufacture dates.

Body type

DfT’s classification of vehicles into cars, light goods vehicles, motorcycles, buses and coaches, heavy goods vehicles and other vehicles (Chapter 3).

CAZ

Clean Air Zone: an area in which the most polluting vehicles are charged or restricted (Chapter 4).

Churn

The change in the vehicles in an area from year to year as vehicles arrive, move and leave.

DfT

Department for Transport.

DVA

Driver & Vehicle Agency, Northern Ireland.

DVLA

Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which keeps the vehicle register.

DVSA

Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency, which runs the MOT scheme.

Euro standard

A European limit on the air pollutants a new vehicle may emit (Chapter 4).

First-use date

The date a vehicle was first used on the road, normally its first registration.

Generic model

DfT’s grouping of model variants under one name, such as FORD FIESTA.

HGV

Heavy goods vehicle: a goods vehicle over 3.5 tonnes.

LGV

Light goods vehicle: a goods vehicle up to 3.5 tonnes; a van or pick-up.

MAUP

Modifiable areal unit problem: results from area data depend on the size and shape of the areas (Chapter 7).

MOT test

The annual roadworthiness test for vehicles three years old and over (Chapter 1).

Observed

In CARS, a vehicle is observed in a year when it has a postcode area in that year.

OGL

Open Government Licence.

Parquet

A compressed, column-based file format for large tables.

PCA

Postcode area: the one or two letters at the start of a postcode (Chapter 7).

PHEV

Plug-in hybrid electric vehicle.

Plausible mileage

An annual mileage the annualisation judged believable (legit_mileage_YYYY = TRUE).

SORN

Statutory Off Road Notification: a declaration that a vehicle is kept off the road (Chapter 6).

Test class

The class of MOT test a vehicle takes (Chapter 3).

Type approval

Certification that a vehicle design meets the rules for its category (M1, N1 and so on) (Chapter 3).

V5C

The vehicle registration certificate, or logbook.

VES

The DVLA’s Vehicle Enquiry Service.

VRM

Vehicle registration mark: the registration number (Chapter 5).

WLTP, NEDC

The laboratory tests used to measure official fuel consumption and CO2; WLTP replaced NEDC in 2017–2018.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
section: C.2 How data gets into the book
text:
C.2 How data gets into the book
Nothing in the book reads the pipeline repository directly. Instead:

data/manifest.yml lists every file the book uses from MOT-pipline.
scripts/sync-pipeline.R copies those files into data/pipeline/ (data) and reports/ (the pipeline’s reports, shown as appendices), and records the pipeline’s commit in data/pipeline/provenance.csv.
scripts/run-examples.R runs each query in sql/ against the vehicle table and saves the result in data/examples/. The worked examples display the same .sql files, so the code shown is exactly the code that produced the results.
scripts/run-coverage.R counts, for every column of the vehicle table, how many vehicles have a value, by year of first use and by year, and saves the counts in data/coverage/ for the coverage sections of the data dictionary. scripts/run-values.R likewise summarises each column’s values over time, in data/values/, for the dictionary’s Values sections.
Chapters read the copies with read_pipeline() and read_example() from R/book.R, and compute every number, table and chart from them when the book is rendered.

The copies are committed, so anyone can rebuild the book without access to the pipeline or the 9 GB vehicle table.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
section: C.3 Updating after a new pipeline build
text:
C.3 Updating after a new pipeline build
From the book’s root folder, with MOT-pipline checked out alongside it (or MOT_PIPELINE_DIR set to its location):
Rscript scripts/sync-pipeline.R   # copy the new outputs
Rscript scripts/run-examples.R    # rerun the examples (needs the parquet)
Rscript scripts/run-coverage.R    # recount column coverage (needs the parquet)
Rscript scripts/run-values.R      # resummarise column values (needs the parquet)
Rscript scripts/rebuild.R         # re-execute every chapter and render
Then check the result, and commit data/, reports/ and _freeze/. Pushing to main publishes the book.






ImportantCheck the words, not just the numbers



Numbers in the text are computed, but sentences that interpret them (“the two averages are almost identical”, “most were still tested in Leeds”) are written by hand. After a rebuild, read the chapters whose figures changed and make sure the text still fits.


If a pipeline file used by the book is renamed or removed, the sync script stops with an error naming it. Update data/manifest.yml and the chapter that reads it.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
section: C.4 Why rebuild.R clears the frozen results
text:
C.4 Why rebuild.R clears the frozen results
The book uses Quarto’s freeze option: the results of each chapter’s code are stored in _freeze/ and reused until that chapter’s source changes. This is what lets GitHub Actions publish the book without R. It also means a plain quarto render will not pick up new data, because the chapters themselves have not changed. scripts/rebuild.R deletes _freeze/ so that every chapter runs again.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
section: C.5 Adding pipeline data to a chapter
text:
C.5 Adding pipeline data to a chapter

Add the file to data/manifest.yml.
Run Rscript scripts/sync-pipeline.R.
In the chapter, source("R/book.R") and read it with read_pipeline("outputs", "tables", ...).

To add a worked example, put the query in sql/ (naming the file as 'vehicles_enhanced.parquet'), run Rscript scripts/run-examples.R exNN, and show it with {{< include ../sql/exNN_name.sql >}} inside a sql code block.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
section: C.6 When the vehicle table gains or loses columns
text:
C.6 When the vehicle table gains or loses columns
The data dictionary chapters (chapters/dictionary/) each describe a group of columns, defined once in dict_groups in R/book.R. A column that has been removed stops the render with an error naming it. A new column is listed in a warning on the part’s opening page until it is added to a group, and to that chapter’s overview text. Rerun scripts/run-coverage.R and scripts/run-values.R after either change. A column whose values should be charted as categories although it is stored as a number belongs in dict_coded.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
text:
C.7 Writing conventions

Placeholders for material still to come are callouts titled To be written (or To be confirmed for statements to check), with the class .todo. Search the chapters for .todo to list them.
Pitfalls are callouts titled Pitfall: …, and each is also summarised in



Charts use theme_cars() and the palette in R/book.R, with at most four series each.

title: Appendix C — Maintaining this book
text:
C.8 Publishing
.github/workflows/publish.yml renders the book from the frozen results and publishes it to the gh-pages branch on every push to main. One-off set-up: run quarto publish gh-pages once locally to create the branch, then in the repository’s settings set GitHub Pages to deploy from the gh-pages branch. The book will then be at cars-project.github.io/documentation.
To preview locally, run quarto preview.

title: Methodology
text:
How to read this document
Generated from reports/methodology.qmd by the MOT-pipline methodology_doc target. Every figure comes from the latest build (profile: main). Edit the template, not this file.
This document describes how MOT-pipline turns the Bristol vehicle-level MOT table into the enhanced vehicle dataset and summary tables. For each stage it sets out what is done, how, and the assumptions behind it, so users of the outputs can judge how far to rely on each column.
The code for each stage is named in its section. Column-level definitions are in outputs/data_dictionary.csv, which the pipeline writes. The pipeline was audited end to end in October 2026; pipeline_audit.md records what was checked, what was found and what changed.
It is written for two readers. If you use the outputs but not the code, read the plain-language summary below, then the Assumptions paragraph at the end of each section and the summary table in Section 12: they say what each column and table can and cannot support. You do not need to read SQL. If you maintain the code, each section starts with the file that implements it, and the table below maps every stage to its code and its targets target, so you can go from a sentence here to the function that does it.
