3. The vocabulary, pedantically
legit_mileage is Bristol’s judgement, and it has three states, not two. TRUE is a mileage it judged plausible. A blank is a mileage it did not assess. FALSE means it judged the mileage implausible and removed it, so a FALSE row never carries a mileage; n_mileage_removed counts those vehicles. Totals in this report are plausible mileage unless they say otherwise, and section 4.2 gives the size of the unassessed group year by year.
A postcode area is pca_YYYY: either a real area, or one of unborn (before the vehicle existed), dead (after its last MOT, which begins about two years after the last test because Bristol carries the area forward) or unknown (a year inside its life with no area recorded; rare, because Bristol back-fills a new vehicle’s years before its first MOT with its first test’s area). “Observed” in this report means a real area, not necessarily a test.
body_type is the DfT body type attached in Stage 2, not the MOT test class, so it exists for vehicles with no test class.
The charts group it as Cars, Light goods vehicles, Motorcycles and Other, with everything else in Other.
fuel_simple is the harmonised fuel in six groups, which separates plug-in hybrids from other hybrids; every table uses it, as the churn tables do. test_class is the harmonised MOT test class (the anonymised class, else that of similar vehicles), as in the churn tables.
Age is the number of whole years between the first use date and 1 June of the year, as in the churn tables. A vehicle first used after 1 June has a negative age; those are counted separately rather than dropped (n_negative_age). The age table caps age at 40 and holds every negative age at -1 (the churn tables’ <0).
Mileage bands in mileage_distribution_by_year_body.csv are named by their lower edge in miles: bands of 1,000 up to 50,000, then three wider bands, with negative mileage at -1000.

text:
10. Comparison with DfT small-area counts
DfT publishes vehicle counts for small areas (LSOAs and their equivalents) in tables VEH0125 (all vehicles by body type, keepership and licence status), VEH0135 (ultra low emission vehicles) and VEH0145 (plug-in vehicles). data-raw/build_dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.R takes these tables from the PlaceBasedCarbonCalculator build, where the counts DfT suppresses are reconstructed, and adds them up to postcode areas (inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv). The tables give the first quarter of each year, so MOT year Y is compared with DfT counts at the end of March of Y + 1. DfT counts here are licensed and SORN vehicles together.
The two sources are not expected to agree exactly. DfT counts include vehicles under three whose first MOT is not yet in the data (once it is, Bristol back-fills their area), and the MOT data keeps a vehicle in its area for two years after its last test, after DfT has stopped counting it if it was scrapped. DfT also places a vehicle at its keeper’s address, so company and lease cars are counted where the company is registered, while the MOT data places a vehicle where it was observed. The maps and tables below therefore compare each postcode area with the national ratio for 2022 (1.040 MOT cars per DfT car).

Figure 18. Vehicles observed in the MOT data each year divided by DfT’s licensed and SORN count at the end of March of the following year (VEH0125, summed from small areas to postcode areas in inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv), by body group. At 1 (grey line) the two count the same.

Figure 19. For each postcode area in 2022, its ratio of MOT cars to DfT cars relative to the national ratio (1.040). Blue: more cars in the MOT data than the national ratio suggests; red: fewer. The colour scale stops at 40% either way.

Figure 20. The share of each postcode area’s DfT cars kept by a company (VEH0125 keepership), 2022. High shares mark areas where fleet and lease cars are registered.

Figure 21. Each point is a postcode area in 2022: its DfT cars against its MOT cars, on log scales, coloured by the share of its DfT cars kept by a company. The grey line is the national ratio; labelled areas differ from it by more than 25%.

12. Source files and how to rebuild
Every table this document describes is listed with its grain and contents in section 2.1, and every column of every one of them in section 2.2. Two further inputs are read directly by the charts and maps:

inputs/dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.csv: DfT VEH0125, VEH0135 and VEH0145 by postcode area (data-raw/build_dft_lsoa_vehicles_by_pca.R).
inputs/postcode_areas_100m.gpkg: postcode area boundaries simplified to 100 m (data-raw/build_postcode_area_boundaries.R).

The tables and this document are built by targets, so rebuilding only repeats what changed:
# the mileage tables, their measurements and this report
targets::tar_make(names = c("mileage_tables", "mileage_area_tables",
                            "mileage_profile_tables", "mileage_report"))

# just this document, from the tables already written
targets::tar_make(names = "mileage_report")
Editing reports/mileage_report.qmd re-renders this document only. Editing R/summary_mileage.R rebuilds the tables and then this document. Every number above is read from the files listed in section 2.1 and the measurements in outputs/quality/mileage_profile/, so nothing here can drift from the build it describes.

section: 13. Things to be careful about, in one place
text:
13. Things to be careful about, in one place







Issue
Detail




The last year is partial
2025 holds 25,803,313 vehicle-years with a recorded mileage against 36,734,471 in 2024, and 0.03% of that mileage was never assessed. Do not read a trend into the final year.


Young vehicles are missing from the recent years
A vehicle’s mileage is only known once it has had an MOT, at three years old; Bristol then estimates the earlier years from that test. So the youngest ages fill in only once the first test is in the data and empty out towards the end of the series, and the vehicles that do appear there are the ones tested unusually early. Section 11 quantifies it.


Unassessed mileage is not zero mileage
Bristol removed the mileage it judged implausible, so a recorded mileage is either plausible or unassessed. Treating the unassessed as zero would lose 8,170 vehicle-years in 2025 alone.


A growing share of the fleet has no location
The unknown group reaches 12,640,179 vehicles by 2025. They are in the vehicle counts and in no postcode area row, so the area rows do not sum to the fleet.


The mileage is Bristol’s, not ours
Annual mileage, the postcode area and the plausibility flag all come from Bristol’s annualisation and are taken as given. The pipeline applies no scaling and does not re-derive them.


One definition of age, test class and fuel
Every table uses the churn tables’ definitions: age at 1 June, the harmonised test_class and the harmonised fuel_simple. Until October 2026 the test class and fuel tables used the columns as supplied (test_class_ANON, fuel_DVSA) and age was the calendar-year difference, so older copies of these tables are not directly comparable.


Vehicles with no body type
2,922,885 vehicles (3.13%) have no DfT body type, all of them vehicles with no MOT test class. They are grouped as Other rather than dropped.


Vehicles with no age
123 vehicles (0%) have no first use date, so they appear in the vehicle and mileage tables but in no age table.


Vehicles with no test class
5,510,998 vehicles (5.9%) have no test class and are absent from the test class tables, which therefore total less than the fleet.


Negative and very large mileage
Over the whole series 0 vehicle-years carry a mileage below zero and 105,523 above 50,000. Both are left in the published tables and counted separately (n_negative_mileage, n_over_50k_mileage) rather than removed.


Negative ages are not all errors
n_negative_age in the area table counts every year before a vehicle was first used, and every vehicle first used after 1 June of the year, so it is large by construction and is not a count of errors. Among vehicles actually observed in a postcode area, 26,120,435 have a negative age, nearly all first used later in the year.


A mean has a changing denominator
A mean mileage is over the vehicles that have a recorded mileage, not over the fleet, and that denominator changes year by year. The tables carry counts and totals rather than means alone, so a mean can be recomputed over any chosen group.

title: Churn tables: what each one contains and exactly how it was made

1. What this document is for
Generated from reports/churn_tables_report.qmd by the MOT-pipline churn_tables_report target (profile: main). Edit the template, not this file: every number below is recomputed from the data each time the pipeline runs.
The churn tables answer the question “do vehicles stay in the same part of the country, and does that differ by age, mileage, fuel or engine size?” There are 73 CSV files in outputs/tables/churn/. This document explains, for each one:
No programming knowledge is assumed. Where a rule is fussy, the fussy version is given rather than a simplified one, because the simplified version is where mistakes come from. Column and file names appear like this.

text:
2. The short version

Every table is built from one intermediate file, outputs/intermediate/churn_base.parquet, which has one row per vehicle (81,112,156 vehicles) and one column per year for location and mileage.
A vehicle’s location in a year is a postcode area (“LS”, “BS”, “BT”), or one of three words standing in for “no location recorded”: unborn, dead, unknown.
Almost every table counts vehicles grouped by postcode area, and splits them either by year or by a characteristic (age, mileage, fuel, engine size, emissions category).
The biggest limitation is not missing data in the usual sense: it is what a “location” is. Bristol gives a vehicle a postcode area in every year from its first registration to two years after its last MOT: the years before the first MOT (at age three) copy the first test’s area, and the two years after the last one carry it on. So a vehicle’s area in a year is not always a year in which it was tested there, and a scrapped vehicle stays in its area’s stock for about two years (section 5 and section 12). In 2019, the best covered year, 52.3% of the churn-base vehicles had a postcode area.
The pipeline cross-checks every count that two tables should agree on (outputs/quality/cross_checks.csv, summarised in the data quality report): the Set 2 stock, Set 1b, Set 1d, Set 3, Set 4, Set 7A and Set 7B totals all reconcile with the churn base.

Identifiers and dates copied or derived from the cleaned file.

title: Churn tables: what each one contains and exactly how it was made
text:
5. The vocabulary, pedantically
Postcode area (PCA) - the letters at the start of a UK postcode: “BS” for Bristol, “LS” for Leeds. There are about 120 of them. Northern Ireland is the single area BT (earlier deliveries called it NI).
A real postcode area - any value that is not unborn, dead or unknown. The phrase is used throughout: “vehicles in a real PCA in 2017” means vehicles whose location in 2017 was actually known.
unborn / dead / unknown - filled in where no postcode area was recorded, by these rules, in this order:

unborn if the vehicle’s birth_date year is later than the year in question;
dead if the vehicle’s last MOT year is earlier than the year in question;
unknown otherwise - alive, but not observed.

A vehicle with no dates at all is treated as already born.
Status in a comparison - when a table compares a vehicle’s location in one year against a reference year, the answer is one of four words, tested in this order:







Status
Meaning




dead
the comparison year says dead


unborn
the comparison year says unborn


same
a real postcode area, the same as the reference year


different
anything else: a genuinely different area, or unknown, or - where the reference year is the earlier one (Sets 1b, 1c) - a reference-year status of unborn, unknown or dead



The last row is the single most important caveat in this document. different means “not demonstrably in the same place”, not “moved”. Two things other than a move put a vehicle in it:

A vehicle not located in the comparison year (unknown) is counted as different, not as missing. This is rare: 33,656 vehicles arrived in an area in 2018 from unknown or dead.
In Sets 1b and 1c a new vehicle is different. The status describes the later year against the earlier one, so a vehicle that was unborn a year earlier and is now in an area is different - it did not move, it was registered. In 2018, 2.57M of the 8.57M different vehicles in Set 1b (lag 1) were new vehicles; 5.97M had moved from another area. Set 1d separates these flows; use it for any statement about moving.

A move - a change of postcode area between two consecutive years where both years hold a real postcode area. A vehicle going LS → unknown → BD is recorded as no moves, because neither pair of consecutive years has two real areas. This makes the move counts conservative: real moves across a gap in observation are not counted.
Age - whole years at 1 June of the year in question, calculated as the days from the first use date to 1 June divided by 365.25, rounded down. A vehicle first used in August 2013 is age 3 in 2017, not 4. Ages can be negative (a first use date after the year), which is why the age bands include a <0 band.
Movement rate - the churn v2 definition, n_moves_2007_2017 / (age in 2017 - 3), defined for vehicles aged 4 or over in 2017. The idea was “moves per year of life after the first three, when a car has no MOT”. It does not measure that, for two reasons, and it should not be compared across ages:

Bristol back-fills a vehicle’s postcode area into the years before its first MOT, so those years are “located” and a move between them can be counted (though, being copies, they rarely show one). The numerator therefore counts moves over up to ten year pairs (2007-2017) while the denominator counts years of life after the third.
For a vehicle aged 4 the denominator is 1 but there are about 4.5 observed year pairs; for a vehicle aged 20 it is 17 but there are at most 10.

In this build the mean churn v2 rate falls from 0.47 at age 4 to 0.05 at age 20 and over, while the windowed rate stays between 0.1 and 0.2 at every age: the fall is produced by the formula, not by the vehicles. The churn v2 rate is larger than the windowed rate below age 13 and smaller above it. Windowed movement rate divides by the number of year pairs where both years hold a real area (n_moves_2007_2017 / n_obs_2007_2017), so it measures moves per observed year and is the one to quote. Note that the observed pairs include the back-filled years before the first MOT and the two years after the last one, in which no move can appear, so even the windowed rate understates the rate at which vehicles that are on the road change area.
Static - a vehicle in a real postcode area in 2017 that was in the same area in 2016 and 2018. A vehicle unknown in 2016 is therefore not static, even if it never moved: non-static mixes movers with vehicles not located in 2016 or 2018 (or dead by 2018). Of the 2017 cohort aged 4+, 64.8% were static.
Bands - every band includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound. Engine size 2000cc falls in 1700-2000; 2001cc falls in >2000. Mileage 12,000 falls in >12k, not 5-12k. Engine size 0 has a band of its own, 0 (electric), because the harmonised engine size is 0 for the fuels with no engine; the lowest size band starts at 1cc and says so.
Every band set used anywhere in the churn tables is spelled out here, so that a column heading in a CSV can always be traced back to a rule:

Every band set
bands lists the band labels in the order the tables put them in. A vehicle whose value is missing gets no band at all: in a wide table it lands in the NA column, and in a per-category table it is dropped.

The NA column - several wide tables have a final column headed NA. That is not an error: it counts vehicles whose characteristic is unknown (usually engine size or mileage). Tables that list one row per category instead drop the unknown category. So a band table and its matching cross-tab can have slightly different totals, and the difference is the unknowns.
Zeros - every combination of area, year and band appears in the wide tables, filled with 0 where no vehicle matched. A 0 means “none”, not “not measured”.
Rounding - counts are exact. Proportions in Sets 2 and 6 are written at full precision. Average mileages in Set 7A are rounded to one decimal place; percentages in Set 0 to two.

text:
6. How complete the variables are
The table in section 4.1 gives the exact missing counts. In words, for the 81,112,156 vehicles:

Location and fuel are never missing. Every vehicle has a value in every pca_YYYY column (though 49.0% of 2017’s values are one of the three stand-in words), and every vehicle has a fuel group.
Engine size is missing for 6,232 vehicles (0.0%), so the four engine band columns are missing for exactly the same vehicles.
Euro status is missing for 3,888,410 vehicles (4.8%); in the harmonised column these hold the reason instead (pre_euro, no_schedule or no_date), so count them by euro_status_src, not by an empty euro_status. That looks like good coverage, but most of it is an assumption rather than a record: the register holds a Euro status for only a minority of vehicles, and where it holds none the enhanced table fills in the standard that was compulsory for new registrations of that body type when the vehicle was made (methodology.md, Section 5.7). Euro status is used only in the Set 7 check table.
Movement rate is missing for 30,878,242 vehicles (38.1%) - those aged under 4 in 2017, for whom it is not defined.
birth_pca (the area a vehicle first appeared in) is missing for 41,617,674 vehicles (51.3%): vehicles already registered before the data starts never have an unborn-to-area transition to read it from. Set 4’s “born here” columns are only meaningful for recent vehicles.
The dates behind the age calculation are never missing in the combined first_use_date, but the individual sources are: DVSA’s own date is missing for 10,093,594 vehicles (12.4%), which is what Set 0 reports on.

title: Churn tables: what each one contains and exactly how it was made
section: 9. The tables, one set at a time
text:
9. The tables, one set at a time
Each set below says: the question, the vehicles counted, the variables, the grouping, the arithmetic, and the files, and ends with graphs drawn from its CSVs in outputs/tables/churn/ as written by this build. A map of a table that covers every year shows 2022, the latest year whose fleet is complete (vehicles first tested in the most recent years are not all back-filled yet); grey areas have no vehicles in the table.

Set 0 - where the first use date came from

Question. How much of the age calculation rests on DVSA’s own date?
Vehicles. All 81,112,156.
Variables. firstUsedDate_DVSA, monthOfFirstRegistration_DVLA, birth_date.
Grouping. None. Four counts, one per source, by the first rule that applies: DVSA’s date if present, else DVLA’s first registration, else birth_date, else none.
Arithmetic. pct is the count over all vehicles, to two decimals. n_differs_from_v1_birthDate, on the first row only, counts vehicles whose DVSA first use date is not the same day as birth_date - a measure of how much the earlier version of this analysis, which used birth_date, differed.
File. set0_first_use_date_provenance.csv.


Figure 2. The four counts of set0_first_use_date_provenance.csv: the source of each vehicle’s first use date, as a share of the churn base, labelled with the vehicles behind each share.


Set 1 - who is still where they were

Question. Of the vehicles in area X in a reference year, how many are in the same area, a different one, dead or not yet born, in each later year?
Vehicles. All of them, including those whose reference-year location is dead, unborn or unknown - except in set1a2, which keeps only vehicles in a real area in 2017 (41,341,397 vehicles).
Variables. pca_YYYY for every year, test_class, and age for the age4plus variants.
Grouping. Row = reference-year postcode area (plus test class). For each year, every vehicle is labelled same, different, dead or unborn against the reference year, and the labels are counted.
Arithmetic. Counts only. The table is then pivoted so each status-and-year pair becomes a column, named status_year (for example same_2019), ordered by year then status, with missing combinations as 0.
Files and what the reference year is.

set1a_...change_from_2017.csv - reference year 2017, all vehicles. Rows include dead, unborn and unknown as reference locations.
set1a2_..._cohort_only.csv - the same, restricted to vehicles in a real area in 2017. This is the one to use for “of the 2017 fleet, how many stayed”.
set1b_...from_year-N.csv for N = 1, 2, 3 - a rolling comparison: each year against the area N years earlier. The row label is the later year’s area, so a vehicle contributes to different rows in different years.
set1c_...from_year-N_age4plus.csv for N = 1, 2 - as 1b, but only vehicles aged 4 or over in the later year, which removes the cars-with-no-MOT-yet effect.
set1d_pca_flows_year-1.csv - the year-on-year flows behind 1b (lag 1), one row per year and area: stock_prev (in the area a year earlier), stayed, out_moved (now in another area), out_dead, out_unobserved, in_moved (from another area), in_new (unborn a year earlier), in_reappeared (unknown or dead a year earlier) and stock_now. Exactly, stock_prev = stayed + out_moved + out_dead + out_unobserved and stock_now = stayed + in_moved + in_new + in_reappeared; nationally, in_moved equals out_moved. Added in the October 2026 audit.

Traps. unknown is inside different, and in 1b and 1c so are new vehicles (section 5): 1b’s different is not a count of movers - Set 1d’s in_moved is. The test_class column is constant (4) because of the class filter; it is kept so the file shape matches the earlier analysis.


Figure 3. The 41,341,397 vehicles in a real postcode area in 2017, by their status against their 2017 area in every year: the set1a2 counts summed over areas, as a share of the cohort. different includes unknown, vehicles not located that year.

Figure 4. For each year and lag, different / (different + same), summed over the rows of Sets 1b and 1c whose row (the later year’s area) is a real postcode area. different includes new vehicles and vehicles seen again after a gap, not only movers; Set 1d, in the next figure, separates them.

Figure 5. The year-on-year flows of set1d_pca_flows_year-1.csv summed over all areas, with the flows into areas above zero and those out of them below. Nationally the two moved flows are equal. The dead flow lags scrapping by about two years, because Bristol keeps a postcode area for two years after the last MOT, and new vehicles of the last two or three years are missing until their first MOT is in the data.

Figure 6. Net migration between postcode areas in 2022: (in_moved - out_moved) / stock_prev for each area in set1d_pca_flows_year-1.csv. New and scrapped vehicles are left out. The colour scale runs from -3% to +3%.


Set 2 - counts by characteristic, and who stayed put
Set 2 has two unrelated halves.
Part 1: stock counts by area, year and band.

Vehicles. All vehicles that were in a real area in the year being counted; the population therefore changes from year to year.
Variables and bands. Age at that year (22 bands, <0 to 20+); mileage that year (27 bands of 1,000 miles); fuel_simple (6 groups); engine size in three different band sets - the detailed one (26 bands), 100cc bands (37 bands) and 4 bands (5 bands).
Grouping. Row = year and postcode area. Column = band.
Arithmetic. Counts. Absent combinations are filled with 0, and a final NA column holds vehicles whose band is unknown.
Files. set2_pca_ageband_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv, set2_pca_mileageband_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv, set2_pca_fuel_type_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv, set2_pca_engine_size_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv, set2_pca_engine_size_100cc_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv, set2_pca_engine_size_4band_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv.


Figure 7. The share of each year’s located vehicles in each band of four of the stock tables above (set2_pca_*_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv), summed over all areas. Grey is a missing value (the NA column). Age and mileage bands run from dark (low) to light (high); the 27 mileage bands are not labelled.

Figure 8. The share of each postcode area’s located vehicles in 2022 that are Electric or Plug-in Hybrid Electric, from set2_pca_fuel_type_vehicle_counts_by_year.csv. Plug-in hybrids are a floor: only those the DfT fuel detail identifies are counted (methodology.md, Section 5.5).
Part 2: the share of a 2017 cohort that stayed put.

Vehicles. The 2017 cohort: in a real area in 2017 and aged 4 or over (29,319,667 vehicles, 36.1% of the base). Every “static” and “movement rate” number in Sets 2, 3 and 6 uses this same cohort.
Variables. static_2017, and the 2017 values of age band, mileage band, fuel and engine band.
Grouping. One row per category, or one row per pair of categories for the cross-tabulations.
Arithmetic. n_total is the vehicles in the category; n_static those in the same area in 2016, 2017 and 2018; prop_static is one divided by the other. Vehicles whose category is unknown are excluded here, rather than given an NA column.
Files. set2_static_by_ageband.csv, ..._by_mileageband_detail.csv, ..._by_mileageband_3.csv, ..._by_fuel.csv, ..._by_engine_3band.csv, ..._by_engine_4band.csv, ..._by_engine_100cc.csv, plus seven pairwise cross-tabulations as set2_cross_<pair>_long.csv (one row per cell, with counts) and set2_cross_<pair>_wide_prop.csv (a grid of proportions only).
Trap. prop_static is sensitive to observation, not just to moving: a vehicle not seen in 2016 cannot be static. Compare like with like (similar ages), or use Set 6’s movement rates instead. The share static is drawn beside the movement rates under Set 6.



Set 3 - what a 2017 area’s stock is made of

Question. For each area, where did its 2017 vehicles come from, and where did they go?
Vehicles. In a real area in 2017, all ages (41,341,397 vehicles) - note this is a wider population than Set 2 part 2.
Variables. Status in 2016 and in 2018 against 2017; mileage 2017; age 2017; fuel3; engine_band4; movement_rate.
Grouping. One row per postcode area.
Arithmetic. total_vehicles_2017 is the row’s whole stock. The nine columns from same16_same18 to same16_dead18 are a full 3 × 3 table of 2016 status against 2018 status, so they add up to the total, and residual_other is the total minus those nine (it should be 0; the pipeline prints a warning if any row’s is not). The remaining columns are counts in mileage, fuel, engine and age bands, plus average age, average mileage and average movement rate. arrived_and_left_2016_2018 repeats one of the nine cells under an older name.
Files. set3_pca_components_2017.csv, set3_movement_rate_distribution_2017.csv (the overall distribution across 9 rate bands) and set3_movement_rate_distribution_2017_by_pca.csv (the same split by area). Both distribution tables count only vehicles that have a movement rate.
Note on the engine columns. n_engine_zero is the no-engine band; n_engine_lt1400 keeps its name from the earlier version but now counts 1-1399cc, with electric vehicles in n_engine_zero instead; n_engine_unknown counts vehicles with no engine size.


Figure 9. The share of each postcode area’s 2017 vehicles, of all ages, that were in the same area in 2016, 2017 and 2018: same16_same18 / total_vehicles_2017 in set3_pca_components_2017.csv.

Figure 10. The nine columns of set3_pca_components_2017.csv that split the 2017 stock by 2016 status against 2018 status, summed over all areas, with each one’s share of the total. arrived16 and the 2018 different include vehicles not located in that year (unknown), not only movers.

Figure 11. The vehicles located in 2017 that have a churn v2 movement rate (those aged 4+), by rate band (set3_movement_rate_distribution_2017.csv; _by_pca splits it by area). Rates above 1 are possible because moves before age 3 are counted but those years are not.


Set 4 - electric vehicles by area

Question. Where are the EVs, where did they come from, and do they move differently?
Vehicles. Two groups, joined on the area: columns beginning ev_2017_ describe EVs in a real area in 2017 (44,579 vehicles); columns beginning ev_2022_, nonev_ or all_ describe every vehicle in a real area in 2022 (41,773,660).
Variables. is_ev (fuel exactly Electric - Electric Diesel counts as a hybrid and is excluded), pca_YYYY, birth_pca, ever_moved_pca, mileage_2022, movement_rate_2022.
Grouping. One row per postcode area, sorted by 2022 EV count, highest first.
Arithmetic. Counts, plus mean_movement_rate_2022 averaged over the n_2022_age4plus vehicles old enough to have a rate. Two groups of columns each split a total exactly: ev_2017_left_by_2022 = ev_2017_moved_pca_by_2022 + ev_2017_dead_or_unknown_2022 and ev_present_2022 = ev_2022_born_here_never_moved + ev_2022_born_here_but_moved + ev_2022_not_born_in_this_pca.
File. set4_electric_vehicles_by_pca.csv.
Traps. ever_moved_pca looks at every year, so a move after 2022 still keeps a vehicle out of born_here_never_moved. And birth_pca is unknown for 51.3% of vehicles, all of them older ones, so “born here” is only a fair measure for recent EVs.


Figure 12. The battery electric share of each postcode area’s located vehicles in 2022: ev_present_2022 / (ev_present_2022 + nonev_present_2022) in set4_electric_vehicles_by_pca.csv. Plug-in hybrids are not EVs here.

Figure 13. The electric vehicles located in 2022, split by the three ev_2022_ columns of set4_electric_vehicles_by_pca.csv that add up to ev_present_2022, summed over areas. A vehicle’s birth area is the first area it was located in after being unborn; it is unknown for vehicles older than the data.


Set 5 - does moving area change mileage?

Question. Do vehicles that arrive in a new area drive more or less than those that stayed?
Vehicles. In a real area in 2017 (41,341,397), split into three groups by their 2016 state: stayed_2016_2017 (real area in 2016, same as 2017), arrived_from_other_pca_2016 (real area in 2016, different), and unborn_2016. Vehicles unknown or dead in 2016 fall into none of the three and are dropped.
Variables. mileage_2016, mileage_2017, and the 3-band mileage grouping.
Grouping. One row per group - three rows in total, not one per area.
Arithmetic. Average mileage in each year (over vehicles with a recorded mileage, so the three groups have different denominators), plus counts in the <5k, 5-12k and >12k bands for both years, and the two denominators, n_with_mileage_2016 and n_with_mileage_2017. A vehicle new in 2017 has almost never a 2016 mileage, so unborn_2016’s 2016 average is over a handful of vehicles and should not be quoted.
File. set5_move_vs_mileage.csv.
Trap. The arrivals group is younger on average than the stayers, and younger cars drive more. This table does not adjust for that.


Figure 14. The mean annual mileage in 2016 and 2017 of the three groups of set5_move_vs_mileage.csv, each over the vehicles with a mileage that year (n). Not adjusted for age: arrivals are younger than stayers.


Set 6 - movement rates by characteristic

Question. The same questions as Set 2 part 2, but measured by how often a vehicle moves rather than by whether it sat still across three years.
Vehicles. The same 2017 cohort (29,319,667 vehicles).
Variables. movement_rate and movement_rate_window, by age band, mileage band, fuel and engine band.
Grouping. One row per category, and seven pairwise cross-tabulations.
Arithmetic. n_total is the vehicles in the category; n_with_rate those with a movement rate; the two means are averaged over n_with_rate, not over n_total.
Files. set6_moverate_by_*.csv and set6_cross_*_long.csv / set6_cross_*_wide_mean.csv.
Which rate to quote. The windowed one. mean_movement_rate (churn v2) falls with age by construction (section 5), so a table by age band, or by anything correlated with age (mileage, fuel, engine size), shows that artefact rather than a difference in behaviour. The first figure below draws the two side by side.


Figure 15. For the 29,319,667 vehicles in a real area in 2017 and aged 4+, by category of six characteristics: the share static 2016-2018 (prop_static in set2_static_by_*.csv), with 95% Wilson intervals that are mostly narrower than the points, and the windowed and churn v2 mean movement rates (set6_moverate_by_*.csv). The churn v2 rate falls with age by construction (section 5); the windowed rate does not.

Figure 16. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated age band by mileage band (3 bands): the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_age_mileage3_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_age_mileage3_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 17. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated age band by fuel: the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_age_fuel_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_age_fuel_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 18. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated age band by engine size (4 bands): the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_age_engine4_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_age_engine4_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 19. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated mileage band (3 bands) by fuel: the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_mileage3_fuel_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_mileage3_fuel_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 20. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated mileage band (3 bands) by engine size (4 bands): the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_mileage3_engine4_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_mileage3_engine4_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 21. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated fuel by engine size (4 bands): the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_fuel_engine4_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_fuel_engine4_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.

Figure 22. The same 2017 cohort cross-tabulated fuel by engine size (100cc bands): the share static in each cell (left, set2_cross_fuel_engine100_long.csv) and its windowed movement rate (right, set6_cross_fuel_engine100_long.csv). * marks cells with fewer than 1,000 vehicles.


Set 7 - Clean Air Zone categories and leavers

Question. Where are the vehicles a Clean Air Zone would charge, and do they leave?
Vehicles. In a real area in 2018 (42,034,312) for the check and the leavers; for the yearly counts, whoever was in a real area in each year from 2018 to 2023.
Variables. caz_cat, assigned from fuel and first use year by the first rule that matches: petrol first used before 2006 → petrol_pre2006; diesel first used before 2015 → diesel_pre2015; everything else → other. Plus euro_status, mileage, and the 2018 values of age, mileage, fuel and engine band.
Files.

set7_check_caz_category_vs_eurostatus.csv - a check, not a result: how the date-based category lines up with the Euro standard, by category and fuel. It is about the proxy’s credibility, not a count of the fleet - and it is a weak check, because many Euro statuses are themselves worked out from the date the vehicle was made, so the two sides are not independent.
set7_check_caz_proxy_agreement_by_source.csv - the same check as an agreement rate, split by euro_status_src. Only dvla (recorded on the vehicle) and variant / model_year_fuel (the recorded value of similar vehicles) are an independent test of the proxy; euro_schedule rows agree almost by construction. Only about 0.6% of the vehicles have a status recorded on their own record. The independent part shows the petrol proxy is poor: of the petrol_pre2006 cars with a recorded or borrowed standard, only 8.4% are below Euro 4, because many petrol cars of 2001-2005 already met it; for diesel_pre2015 the figure is 76.5%. The petrol_pre2006 counts in Set 7A and 7B therefore overstate the petrol vehicles a Clean Air Zone would charge.
set7a_pca_caz_categories.csv and its long form set7a_pca_caz_category_by_year_long.csv - counts and average mileage by area, category and year, 2018 to 2023. Average mileage is rounded to one decimal place and averaged only over vehicles with a recorded mileage.
set7b_leavers_2018_to_2023_by_*.csv - vehicles in a real area in 2018 that are not in that same area in 2023 (26,793,137 vehicles, 63.7% of the 2018 stock), split six ways: by 2018 mileage band, engine band, fuel, age band, CAZ category, and by outcome. In the outcome file the same and unborn columns are present but always 0, because a leaver is by definition not in the same area, and a vehicle in a real area in 2018 cannot be unborn later; the counts are therefore in different and dead.

Trap. “Leaver” includes vehicles that were scrapped, and vehicles simply not observed in 2023. The by-outcome file is the one that separates those: dead is scrapped, different is elsewhere or unobserved.


Figure 23. The vehicles located each year by Clean Air Zone proxy category, summed over areas from set7a_pca_caz_category_by_year_long.csv. The category comes from fuel and first use year, not the recorded Euro standard, and petrol_pre2006 overstates the petrol vehicles a zone would charge.

Figure 24. The share of each postcode area’s located vehicles in 2023 in a chargeable proxy category, petrol first used before 2006 or diesel before 2015 (set7a_pca_caz_category_by_year_long.csv).

Figure 25. The 26,793,137 vehicles in a real area in 2018 but not in that area in 2023, split six ways by the set7b_leavers_2018_to_2023_by_*.csv tables summed over areas: each bar is one table and adds up to 100%, and segments over 6% are labelled. different includes vehicles not located in 2023.

Figure 26. From set7_check_caz_proxy_agreement_by_source.csv: for each proxy category and fuel, how often the vehicle’s Euro standard agrees with the proxy, by where the standard came from, sized by the vehicles with a standard. Only dvla (recorded) and variant / model_year_fuel (borrowed from similar vehicles) test the proxy; euro_schedule is derived from the date, so it agrees almost by construction.

text:
11. How to rebuild this
The churn tables and this document are built by the pipeline, so they always describe the same run:
# everything
targets::tar_make()

# just the churn tables and this document
targets::tar_make(names = tidyselect::starts_with("churn"))
Changing a setting under churn: in config.yml rebuilds the tables that depend on it and then this document. Editing the band definitions or the documentation text means editing R/summary_churn.R, R/report_churn.R or reports/churn_tables_report.qmd - never the generated .md file, which is overwritten on every run.

title: Churn tables: what each one contains and exactly how it was made
section: 12. Things to be careful about, in one place
text:
12. Things to be careful about, in one place

different includes unknown. In Set 1 and in Set 7B’s outcome table, a vehicle that was simply not seen counts as not being in the same place.
Moves are only counted between two observed years. A move across a gap in observation is invisible, so move counts and movement rates are floors, not estimates.
A location is not always an observation. A car under three has no MOT, and Bristol copies its first test’s postcode area back to its first registration; after the last MOT, the area is carried on for two years before the vehicle becomes dead. So a young vehicle cannot be seen to move before its first test, and a scrapped vehicle stays in its area’s stock for about two years. Against DfT’s licensed + SORN counts, the cars aged 3+ located in a postcode area are 6-19% too many, depending on the year (data quality report, cross-checks). The last two or three years of data are also incomplete, because recent first tests are not yet back-filled.
movement_rate (churn v2) falls with age by construction. Use the windowed rate for any comparison across ages or characteristics (section 5).
Set 1b’s different includes new vehicles, about 30% of it in a typical year. Use Set 1d’s in_moved and out_moved for moves.
Sets 2 part 2, 3 and 6 are about a 2017 cohort (36.1% to 51.0% of all vehicles, depending on the table). They say nothing about vehicles that arrived afterwards.
Unknown characteristics are handled two ways. Wide tables put them in an NA column; per-category tables drop them. Totals between the two differ by exactly that amount.
Averages skip missing values rather than treating them as zero. An average mileage is over vehicles with a recorded mileage; divide the count columns yourself if you want a per-vehicle figure over everybody.
Northern Ireland is one area, BT. It is included unless exclude_ni_rows is TRUE (currently FALSE). Tables built before October 2026 called it NI.
The row label in Set 1b and 1c is the later year’s area, not the earlier one, so the same vehicle can appear under different areas in different columns of one row-set.
Most Euro statuses are assumed, not recorded. A missing Euro status is filled from the date the vehicle was made, so the Set 7 Euro check compares a date-based category with a largely date-based standard.
The fuel groups now separate plug-in hybrids. Plug-in Hybrid Electric is a sixth fuel group, taken from the DfT licensing statistics for the vehicle’s model (methodology.md, Section 5.5). It is a floor: a plug-in hybrid of a model DfT sells both ways, and whose model text did not settle it, still counts as Hybrid Electric. In churn v2 mode (churn.fuel_column = fuel_DVSA) the group is always empty, because the DVSA fuel does not have it.

title: Fleet profile tables
text:
What is counted
The tables in tables/profile/ answer the four analyses in the mileage analysis request: the fleet by year and body type, broken down by vehicle characteristic, counted (Analyses 1 and 3) and averaged over mileage (Analyses 2 and 4), with and without an age band.
They are built by R/summary_profile.R from vehicles_enhanced_maximal.parquet, and cover 2005–2025 for Buses and coaches, Cars, Light goods vehicles and Motorcycles.
A vehicle is in a table for a year when all of these hold:
Age is whole years at 1 June of the year since first use, and the fuel group is the harmonised fuel_simple, both as in the churn tables. A vehicle first used after 1 June of the year is in the <0 age band.
The mileage filter is per vehicle-year, not per vehicle. A vehicle counts in the years its mileage was judged plausible and not in the others, so the same vehicle can appear in 2018 and not in 2019.

title: Fleet profile tables
section: How much of the fleet the tables cover
text:
How much of the fleet the tables cover
The Analysis 1 and 3 “counts” are not fleet counts. They count the vehicle-years that pass the mileage filter, so they are smaller than the number of vehicles on the road, and the shortfall is not random: it is concentrated in the youngest vehicles (no MOT yet) and the most recent years (tests not yet in the data). Engine size is banded on recorded cc, with no rounding
A car recorded as 1,390cc is in <1.4, not in the 1.4 it is sold as. Rounding to the nearest tenth of a litre first would move 7.54M cars, 10.2% of those with an engine size, up a band — 6.69M of them from <1.4 to 1.4-1.7, driven by common capacities such as 1,390cc, 1,360cc, 1,396cc and 1,398cc. Exactly 2,000cc is in 1.7-2.0, as in the churn tables.
The bands differ by body type: litres for cars, vans and buses, and the tax classes for motorcycles.


CO2 of 0 only exists for electric vehicles
A recorded 0 g/km is impossible for anything with an engine, so it is cleared early in the pipeline, before the backfill (R/fuel_engine.R), and the vehicle is filled from similar vehicles instead. The co2 here is therefore either a real value or missing, and only Electric and Fuel Cells vehicles reach the 0 band. co2_check in vehicles_enhanced_maximal.parquet says which vehicles were affected.


CO2 is reported for motorcycles and buses, but barely exists
Read the CO2 rows for these body types with care. They are produced because they were asked for, not because the data supports them. Across the whole fleet 93% of recorded motorcycle CO2 values and 86% of recorded bus values are 0, so once the zeros are treated as missing almost nothing is left, and what remains is not a representative sample. Means and bands for these two body types should not be quoted without this caveat.

SMMT classification coverage, 2025
The RACF reference (uk_fleet_enriched_v2) holds DfT cars only, so the SMMT type is applied to cars and left missing for every other body type (fleet_profile.smmt_body_types). Matching it to vans and minibuses would classify them from whichever car shares their generic model name, which is wrong rather than merely incomplete.
A vehicle takes the SMMT type of its DfT model string where that name is consistent enough (smmt_min_share), and of its generic model otherwise — the same rule as body_type.

title: Fleet profile tables
text:
Known limits

Young vehicles are missing from the recent years
A vehicle’s mileage is only known once it has had an MOT, at three years old; Bristol then estimates the years before the first test from that test’s odometer reading, and copies its postcode area back. So the youngest age bands are filled in only once the first test is in the data, and empty out towards the end of the series. Cars aged 0-2 covered by these tables numbered 6,586,088 in 2019 and 585,661 in 2025.
The 0-2 age band is not usable for the last three years, and the vehicles that do appear there are a biased sample: only those tested unusually early, which tend to be high-mileage ones (taxis, fleet cars). Their mean mileage was 7,597 in 2019 and 8,249 in 2025. For the years before the first test, mileage is an estimate, not a reading, at every age band.
2025 is also a partial year.


Means mix recorded and backfilled values
engine_cc, co2 and revenue_weight are recorded where the DVLA supplied them and otherwise backfilled from the most common value of similar vehicles. For cars, most weights and a large share of CO2 values are borrowed rather than recorded (the data quality report gives the shares). The *_src columns in vehicles_enhanced_maximal.parquet give the provenance per vehicle; the profile tables do not split by it, so a mean is over the mix.
Revenue weight is effectively absent for motorcycles (see the revenue_weight row of the continuous table: almost no motorcycles have one), so revenue_weight should not be read for that body type at all.

Figure 15. The median (line) and interquartile range (band) of each continuous measure of the covered vehicles, by body type and year (profile_continuous_by_year.csv, columns p50, p25 and p75). A year is drawn only where at least 100 vehicles have the measure, which is why some panels are empty. The backfilled measures (engine_cc, co2, revenue_weight) mix recorded and borrowed values.


Buses and coaches are mostly minibuses
There are few of them (22,584 covered in 2025), most of them MOT class 5, so cells split by year, age band and engine size are frequently in single figures.
